cna.title: dm array: validate array block headers on read

scenarios.value:
AV:L - The bug is reached when the kernel reads attacker-crafted dm-array metadata from a local block device during device-mapper activation (dm-cache dm_cache_load_mappings, dm-clone bitset load, or dm-era array resize), not via a network protocol.
AC:L - The attacker fully controls the on-disk array-block header (nr_entries, max_entries, value_size) and can compute a matching checksum, so activation deterministically walks off the dm-bufio buffer; there is no race or attacker-uncontrollable memory layout.
PR:L - Device-mapper ioctls require init-namespace CAP_SYS_ADMIN and are not reachable via user namespaces, but the malformed data is on-disk metadata, so the attacker only needs write access to the backing store (loop file, VM/container disk, iSCSI/NBD LUN) that a dm-cache/dm-era/dm-clone stack is built on.
UI:N - Once corrupt metadata is on the backing store, LVM/udev autoactivation, boot, or reattachment of the volume loads mappings without a separate victim action such as mounting a filesystem or opening a file.
S:U - The out-of-bounds access is confined to kernel dm-bufio metadata buffers on the same host; this is ordinary kernel memory corruption, not a VM escape, IOMMU bypass, or sandbox boundary crossing.
C:H - dm_array_cursor_next() takes its loop bound from on-disk nr_entries while element_at() is unguarded pointer arithmetic, so a too-large count keeps the cursor in one block and reads past the dm-bufio data buffer (typically a 4K slab/page) for every cache block at activation, an unbounded kernel out-of-bounds read.
I:H - Unchecked headers let fill_ablock()/trim_ablock() hit BUG_ON on resize, and out-of-bounds mapping, hint, and bitset values from adjacent kernel memory are installed into the cache policy and then used for origin/cache I/O, giving a memory-corruption integrity primitive.
A:H - Walking off the dm-bufio buffer causes a kernel oops or KASAN panic, and an undersized on-disk max_entries hits BUG_ON in fill_ablock() and trim_ablock() during array resize at activation.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

dm array: validate array block headers on read

array_block_check() validates blocknr and csum and nothing else, while
node_check(), next to it, has bounded the structural fields since both
were written. dm_array_cursor_next() takes its loop bound from the
on-disk nr_entries and element_at() is unguarded pointer arithmetic, so
a count larger than the block holds keeps the cursor in one block while
the index grows past it and the read walks off the dm-bufio buffer --
dm_cache_load_mappings() drives it once per cache block at activation.

Check the header against itself: reject a zero value_size, require
max_entries to equal calc_max_entries() for that value_size and block
size, and require nr_entries to fit. Equality rather than an upper bound,
since a count below the real capacity trips BUG_ON() in fill_ablock() and
trim_ablock(). Metadata dm-array writes satisfies all three.

descriptions.value: A client that has opened and funded a payment channel once can re-present the same signed voucher indefinitely and receive paid resources without any further charge. Operators running mpp as paid-API middleware lose revenue in proportion to how much the client consumes, with nothing in the channel state recording the usage.

descriptions.value:
Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input in ZenHive mpp allows a client holding an open payment channel to obtain paid resources without being charged.

MPP.Session.Actions.accept_voucher/3 in lib/mpp/session/actions.ex treats a voucher whose cumulativeAmount equals the channel's already-accepted cumulative amount as an idempotent success, returning the channel unchanged without calling maybe_spend/2. The credential verifies, the protected resource is served, and spent and units stay where they were. Because the server issues a fresh challenge per request and the credential replay store keys on challenge id and payload, the same signed voucher can be re-presented under every new challenge, so one paid voucher yields an unbounded number of paid units. The path is reachable from any method built on MPP.Session.Method through the Plug, MCP, JSON-RPC and WebSocket transports.

This issue affects mpp: from 0.14.0 before 0.16.2.

cna.title: jackson-core: quadratic backtracking in NumberInput.PATTERN_FLOAT via looksLikeValidNumber() enables ReDoS

solutions.value: Upgrade to com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-core 2.18.11, 2.21.7 or 2.22.3, or to tools.jackson.core:jackson-core 3.1.7 or 3.2.2. The 2.17.x, 2.19.x, 2.20.x and 3.0.x lines received no fix on their own branch and are no longer maintained upstream; consumers of those lines must move forward to a maintained release.

supportingMedia.value: Upgrade to com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-core 2.18.11, 2.21.7 or 2.22.3, or to tools.jackson.core:jackson-core 3.1.7 or 3.2.2. The 2.17.x, 2.19.x, 2.20.x and 3.0.x lines received no fix on their own branch and are no longer maintained upstream; consumers of those lines must move forward to a maintained release.

workarounds.value: Until upgrading, lower StreamReadConstraints.maxStringLength well below its default of 20,000,000 characters so that oversized string tokens are rejected before number coercion, and apply wall-clock timeouts to parse and coercion operations. Because matching cost is quadratic in token length, a tight length bound substantially reduces worst-case cost. These are mitigations, not a complete fix.

descriptions.value:
NumberInput.looksLikeValidNumber() in FasterXML jackson-core pre-validates "stringified numbers" with two regular expressions: PATTERN_FLOAT ([+-]?[0-9]*[\.]?[0-9]+([eE][+-]?[0-9]+)?), present since 2.17.0, and PATTERN_FLOAT_TRAILING_DOT, added in 2.17.2. PATTERN_FLOAT places adjacent quantifiers over the same character class -- an optional [0-9]* run, an optional dot, then a required [0-9]+ run -- so input that ultimately fails to match forces Java's backtracking engine to retry every possible split point of the digit run. 



Matching cost therefore grows with the square of the input length. 



An attacker who can supply JSON that an application deserializes into a numeric target type reaches this method through jackson-databind's default String-to-number coercion (StdDeserializer and NumberDeserializers for BigDecimal, BigInteger, Double and Float). 



Because StreamReadConstraints.maxStringLength defaults to 20,000,000 characters, no constraint bounds the input before it reaches the regex. 



Testing by the reporter confirmed O(n^2) growth across five consecutive input-size doublings, with a single 160,000-character string consuming roughly 74 seconds in one call; a small number of concurrent requests of ordinary body size can therefore exhaust a server's request-handling thread pool. 



The affected method does not exist before 2.17.0, so 2.16.x and earlier releases are not affected. 



The fix replaces both regular expressions with a hand-rolled single-pass scan.

cna.title: AVideo Open Redirect via playlistSort.php Referer Header

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: AVideo Open Redirect via playlistSort.php Referer Header

descriptions.value: AVideo through commit c3edcc274c389816d434acadac07ee78eaf330c1 contains an open redirect in objects/playlistSort.php. Because the endpoint is not a *.json.php script, AVideo's automatic CSRF guard (autoCSRFGuard()/forbidIfIsUntrustedRequest()) does not run, and when the request includes the sort parameter the script issues a Location header set to the unvalidated $_SERVER['HTTP_REFERER'] value without calling isSafeRedirectURL(). A remote unauthenticated attacker can therefore induce a logged-in user who can manage the targeted playlist to submit a cross-origin POST with a crafted Referer, causing the victim's playlist to be reordered and the victim's browser to be redirected from a trusted AVideo URL to an attacker-controlled site for phishing. No patched version is available.

cna.title: JwtVerifierImpl.Verify does not enforce the JWS `crit` header (RFC 7515 §4.1.11)

descriptions.value: gose parsed the JWS `crit` header into `JwsHeader.Crit` and then never read it. RFC 7515 §4.1.11 requires a recipient to reject a JWS whose listed critical extension parameters it does not understand. gose implements no header extensions, so every token carrying a non-empty `crit` should have been rejected — and none were.

cna.title: lockd, nfsd: RCU-protect nlmsvc_ops dispatch

scenarios.value:
AV:N - lockd is the in-kernel NLM RPC server on TCP/UDP (rpcbind-registered) used with nfsd. nlm_do_fopen() and nlm_delete_file() run from NLM LOCK/TEST/UNLOCK/FREE_ALL in svc_recv, so a remote NFS/NLM peer reaches the unguarded nlmsvc_ops->fopen/fclose dispatch.
AC:H - The UAF requires exit_nfsd()/rmmod nfsd to NULL nlmsvc_ops with a plain store and free nfsd .text while lockd still dispatches. A remote attacker can flood NLM requests but cannot unload nfsd; that victim-side module teardown is beyond attacker control.
PR:N - lockd_authenticate() accepts RPC_AUTH_NULL and RPC_AUTH_UNIX before procedure dispatch. nlm_fopen() uses NFSD_MAY_BYPASS_GSS|NFSD_MAY_NLM, and typical exports use AUTH_SYS, so no host account or capability is required.
UI:N - Exploitation is driven by attacker-sent NLM RPCs to an already-running lockd; no victim user must mount a filesystem or open a file. nfsd unload is an environmental timing condition, not User Interaction.
S:U - The module-text UAF and NULL deref corrupt host kernel lockd/nfsd state within the same OS security authority and do not cross a VM, IOMMU, or sandbox boundary.
C:H - After rmmod, a stale nlmsvc_ops load calls fopen/fclose from freed nfsd .rodata/.text. Reclaim of those module pages lets the attacker control the indirect-call target, yielding an arbitrary kernel read per UAF guidance.
I:H - Indirect call through a dangling nlmsvc_binding in freed nfsd module memory is a RIP-hijack primitive; spraying recycled module pages enables arbitrary kernel write and control-flow hijack, so integrity impact is high.
A:H - A stale nlmsvc_ops load after rmmod nfsd is either a NULL deref or a call into unmapped module text; both oops/panic the kernel, so availability impact is high.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

lockd, nfsd: RCU-protect nlmsvc_ops dispatch

nlmsvc_ops is published by nfsd_lockd_init() and cleared by
nfsd_lockd_shutdown() with plain stores, while lockd dereferences
it unguarded from dispatch sites in fs/lockd/svcsubs.c. The pointer
targets nfsd's .rodata and the fopen/fclose callbacks live in nfsd's
.text, so a stale load after rmmod nfsd results in either a NULL
deref or a module-text use-after-free.

Declare nlmsvc_ops as __rcu, publish via rcu_assign_pointer(), clear
via RCU_INIT_POINTER() + synchronize_rcu(). Add a struct module
*owner field to nlmsvc_binding and pin the module across indirect
calls with try_module_get/module_put. When the binding is torn down,
fall back to fput() to avoid leaking struct file references.

cna.title: ceph: bound xattr value length in __build_xattrs()

scenarios.value:
AV:N - The MDS-supplied xattr blob is delivered over the kernel Ceph messenger TCP session in inode replies (parse_reply_info_in → ceph_fill_inode) and CEPH_MSG_CLIENT_CAPS (handle_cap_grant), so a malicious or compromised MDS reaches __build_xattrs() with network protocol data.
AC:L - The attacker fully controls the last attribute's 32-bit value length in the xattr blob; setting it larger than the remaining kvmalloc'd wire bytes reliably records an oversized val_len with no race, special memory layout, or rare kernel config.
PR:N - Exploitation requires only the ability to send crafted MDS replies or cap grants as the remote cluster peer on an established session; no local account, capability, or user-namespace privilege on the victim host is needed.
UI:N - Once CephFS is mounted, MDS replies and cap grants are processed automatically, and ceph_get_acl()/__ceph_getxattr() run on ordinary inode permission checks and xattr queries without a further victim mount or click at exploit time.
S:U - The out-of-bounds heap read, userspace disclosure, and possible oops remain inside the client kernel's own security authority and do not cross a VM, IOMMU, or other distinct trust boundary.
C:H - __set_xattr() stores the oversized length and getxattr memcpy()s that many bytes from the undersized blob into a user buffer (up to XATTR_SIZE_MAX), disclosing adjacent kernel heap including pointers; the in-kernel ACL path can copy still larger extents.
I:N - The bug is an out-of-bounds read into a destination buffer sized from the claimed length (VFS kvzalloc or ceph_get_acl kzalloc); it does not provide an attacker-selected write into kernel memory.
A:H - An oversized value length that extends into unmapped kernel addresses faults the in-kernel memcpy in __ceph_getxattr() or ceph_get_acl(), causing a kernel oops or panic the MDS can trigger repeatedly.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ceph: bound xattr value length in __build_xattrs()

__build_xattrs() decodes the MDS-supplied xattr blob one attribute at a
time. For each attribute it reads a 32-bit name length, advances past the
name bytes, reads a 32-bit value length, records the value pointer, and
advances past the value bytes. The two length fields are read with
ceph_decode_32_safe(), but the value bytes themselves are advanced over
with a bare "p += len" and no ceph_decode_need() check that "len" bytes
remain in the blob.

For every attribute except the last, the next iteration's
ceph_decode_32_safe() on the following name length implicitly verifies
that the previous value did not run past the blob end. The final
attribute has no successor, so its decoded value length is never checked
against the blob bounds. A malicious or compromised metadata server can
set the last attribute's value length larger than the bytes actually
present in the blob.

The blob is a dedicated kvmalloc() allocation sized to the wire length
(ceph_buffer_new() in ceph_fill_inode()). __set_xattr() records the
oversized length in xattr->val_len verbatim, and a later getxattr(2) runs
memcpy(value, xattr->val, xattr->val_len) into a user-supplied buffer,
copying bytes past the end of the allocation back to user space.

Impact: a malicious metadata server discloses adjacent kernel heap bytes
to a local user via getxattr(2) on a CephFS file. Add the missing
ceph_decode_need() so an out-of-bounds value length on the final
attribute fails the decode and returns -EIO instead of being stored.

cna.title: nouveau/gem: reserve the bo in the info ioctl around the vma lookup

scenarios.value:
AV:L - Reached only via local DRM ioctls on a nouveau render node (/dev/dri/renderD*): DRM_IOCTL_NOUVEAU_GEM_INFO (nouveau_gem_ioctl_info→nouveau_gem_info) racing DRM_IOCTL_GEM_CLOSE (nouveau_gem_object_close). Not reachable from network protocols, adjacent radios, or physical buses.
AC:L - The attacker controls both sides of the race with threads that GEM_INFO and GEM_CLOSE the same handle, so close kfree()s the nouveau_vma while info still uses it. Skipping UVMM (legacy GEM_NEW) selects the vulnerable path; no victim timing or rare config is required.
PR:L - NOUVEAU_GEM_INFO and GEM_CLOSE are DRM_RENDER_ALLOW with no DRM_ROOT_ONLY or capability checks. Any unprivileged local user who can open the nouveau render node (typical render/video group or uaccess ACL) can trigger it without init-namespace root.
UI:N - Exploitation needs only the attacker opening their own DRM client, creating a GEM BO, and racing GEM_INFO against GEM_CLOSE on that handle; no separate victim action is required.
S:U - The use-after-free corrupts kernel heap state (struct nouveau_vma) inside the host nouveau driver. Impact stays in the same kernel authority; this is not a VM escape or IOMMU/DMA isolation bypass.
C:H - Use-after-free of struct nouveau_vma lets GEM_INFO read vma->addr after kfree, and concurrent walks of nvbo->vma_list can follow attacker-reused slab objects, enabling kernel memory disclosure as with other UAFs.
I:H - UAF of the VMA plus concurrent list_del/list_del_init on nvbo->vma_list enables heap spraying and list-pointer corruption, supporting arbitrary kernel writes and control-flow hijack as with other kernel UAFs.
A:H - Dereferencing a freed nouveau_vma in GEM_INFO or walking a concurrently deleted vma_list causes a kernel oops/panic; the attacker can repeat the race to crash or hang the system.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nouveau/gem: reserve the bo in the info ioctl around the vma lookup

In the non-uvmm path, there could be a race between the info lookup
finding the vma, and the gem close path closing the vma leading
to a use-after-free.

Spotted with the help of Opus 4.6.

cna.title: sctp: stop processing a packet once its association is deleted

scenarios.value:
AV:N - The UAF is reached from sctp_rcv() when a remote peer sends a bundled SCTP packet (COOKIE-ECHO, SHUTDOWN, SHUTDOWN-ACK, then another chunk) to a listening internet-facing SCTP endpoint; no local syscall or link-local medium is required.
AC:L - The attacker fully controls the four-way handshake and the bundled chunk order that creates, caches, then deletes the association in one packet; forcing that packet onto the socket backlog is done with concurrent associations or recv/accept load the attacker generates, with no victim-only race.
PR:N - COOKIE-ECHO is the unauthenticated SCTP handshake completion using only the INIT-ACK cookie as anti-spoofing; a network peer needs no Linux account, capability, or namespace privilege on the victim host.
UI:N - The kernel automatically processes inbound SCTP chunks in sctp_endpoint_bh_rcv()/sctp_do_sm(); no victim mount, file open, or other interactive action is required.
S:U - Impact is kernel heap use-after-free of sctp_association/sctp_transport on the host; it does not cross a VM, container, or IOMMU boundary.
C:H - After DELETE_TCB the next bundled chunk reads freed asoc->state and other association fields and is passed into sctp_do_sm(); UAF of these slab objects enables heap grooming for arbitrary kernel disclosure.
I:H - The same loop writes last_time_heard on the RCU-freed transport and mutates freed asoc fields (stats, last_data_from) before sctp_do_sm() runs with the dangling pointer, yielding a standard UAF write/control-flow primitive.
A:H - Dereferencing the freed association and transport in the endpoint receive loop can oops or panic the kernel, and a remote peer can repeat the bundled packet against any listening SCTP service.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: stop processing a packet once its association is deleted

sctp_endpoint_bh_rcv() looks the association up only when chunk->asoc is
NULL, and caches the result in chunk->asoc and chunk->transport without
taking a reference.

A packet that matches no association is handed to the endpoint, so a peer
can bundle COOKIE ECHO, SHUTDOWN and SHUTDOWN ACK in one packet. The
COOKIE ECHO creates the association, the SHUTDOWN chunk caches it, and
with the outqueue empty the SHUTDOWN ACK reaches sctp_sf_do_9_2_final(),
so the association and its transports are freed.

The endpoint loop has no counterpart to the asoc->base.dead check in
sctp_assoc_bh_rcv(). The next chunk writes to last_time_heard in the freed
transport and is then passed to sctp_do_sm() with the freed association.
The transport is freed through RCU, so this needs the packet to come off
the socket backlog, where the loop runs in task context.

The endpoint loop cannot do the same check: it holds no reference on the
association, so reading asoc->base.dead would itself be a use-after-free.
Mark the packet for discard in the command interpreter, just before it
deletes the association. That is also before sctp_inq_free() releases the
chunk on the association receive path.

sctp_sf_do_5_2_4_dupcook() issues SCTP_CMD_DELETE_TCB for the temporary
association, while the one the packet belongs to stays alive. A restarting
peer can bundle DATA behind its COOKIE ECHO, so compare against
chunk->asoc and leave that case alone.

cna.title: nfsd: validate symlink target length in NFSv4 CREATE

scenarios.value:
AV:N - The flaw is reached through the in-kernel NFS server (nfsd) when a remote client sends an NFSv4 COMPOUND containing OP_CREATE of type NF4LNK over TCP/UDP port 2049; nfsd4_decode_create() runs during XDR decode of that compound.
AC:L - A client fully controls cr_datalen on the wire; one COMPOUND with an NF4LNK target larger than PATH_MAX but within the RPC payload deterministically forces svcxdr_dupstr()/kmalloc of that size, with no race or attacker-uncontrollable condition.
PR:N - The oversized kmalloc occurs in nfsd4_decode_compound() before SEQUENCE/session checks, PUTFH, fh_verify(), or export flavor enforcement; AUTH_NULL and AUTH_UNIX are accepted at the RPC layer, so an unauthenticated peer that can reach nfsd needs no host credentials.
UI:N - Exploitation requires only attacker-sent NFSv4 COMPOUND RPCs; no administrator or end-user action on the server is needed beyond nfsd already listening.
S:U - Impact is confined to kernel memory consumption on the NFS server within the same security authority; there is no VM escape, IOMMU bypass, or sandbox boundary crossing.
C:N - The defect only copies attacker-supplied symlink-target bytes into a correctly sized kmalloc buffer; there is no out-of-bounds read, use-after-free, or other disclosure primitive.
I:N - There is no memory corruption or attacker-controlled write; the buffer is sized to cr_datalen and is only a temporary copy that filesystems later reject with ENAMETOOLONG.
A:H - Each COMPOUND can force a GFP_KERNEL kmalloc of up to the maximum RPC payload (several MiB) on an nfsd thread until compound teardown; flooding concurrent requests across nfsd threads can exhaust kernel memory and OOM or stall the host.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nfsd: validate symlink target length in NFSv4 CREATE

nfsd4_decode_create() accepts an unbounded cr_datalen from the wire for
NF4LNK symlink targets, allowing a client to force a kmalloc of up to
the maximum RPC payload size (several MiB) per COMPOUND op that persists
until compound teardown.  The VFS rejects oversized targets with
ENAMETOOLONG, but the allocation has already occurred.

Reject cr_datalen == 0 early with nfserr_inval and cr_datalen greater
than NFS4_MAXPATHLEN (PATH_MAX) with nfserr_nametoolong to bound the
allocation.

cna.title: ceph: reject export_targets ranks >= CEPH_MAX_MDS in mdsmap decode

scenarios.value:
AV:N - A crafted MDSMap arrives in CEPH_MSG_MDS_MAP over the Ceph messenger TCP session from a monitor or MDS; extra_mon_dispatch() and mds_dispatch() deliver it to ceph_mdsc_handle_mdsmap() on already-mounted CephFS/Rook/Kubernetes clients without a local syscall.
AC:L - The monitor fully controls each export_targets[] u32; after the first map is stored, a later epoch reaches check_new_map() and set_bit() with an attacker-chosen bit number, overflowing the stack bitmap with no race or special layout.
PR:N - The attacker is the remote Ceph monitor or MDS peer and needs no Linux UID, capability, or init-namespace root on the victim, matching other Ceph client decode CVEs such as CVE-2026-68159.
UI:N - Once CephFS is mounted, MDS maps are subscribed and applied automatically in the ceph-msgr worker; a malicious peer can push a new epoch without any further interactive victim action.
S:U - The stack out-of-bounds write corrupts kernel memory on the Ceph client host only and does not cross a VM, IOMMU, or sandbox security authority.
C:H - set_bit() with an attacker-chosen rank writes past the fixed stack bitmap in check_new_map(), corrupting adjacent kernel stack contents; this memory-corruption primitive can be leveraged for information disclosure.
I:H - The overflow is a stack out-of-bounds write of attacker-selected bits at a u32-controlled offset from the targets[] array, enabling control-flow hijack and arbitrary kernel writes.
A:H - An out-of-range bit index makes set_bit() write off the stack object, causing a KASAN stack-out-of-bounds report or kernel oops/panic that a malicious monitor can repeat with each new map epoch.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ceph: reject export_targets ranks >= CEPH_MAX_MDS in mdsmap decode

MDSMap export_targets entries are monitor controlled. check_new_map()
uses each entry as a bit number in a fixed stack bitmap, so a rank
outside the protocol namespace can make set_bit() write past the end of
the array.

Reject ranks outside CEPH_MAX_MDS while decoding the map. Do not
validate against possible_max_rank here because maps may legitimately
reference ranks beyond a temporarily reduced max_mds.

This is due to the plugin not properly verifying that a user is authorized to perform an action. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with custom-level access and above, to access the full message transcript, thread metadata, and user data of any chat-room thread without authentication. This is only exploitable when the chat room's only_joined_can_read setting retains its default value of '0'.

cna.title: sctp: fix stream->outcnt underflow on duplicate RECONF responses

scenarios.value:
AV:N - A remote SCTP peer’s RECONF chunk is processed by sctp_rcv() then sctp_sf_do_reconf() and sctp_process_strreset_resp() on an established association; kernel guidance treats in-kernel SCTP packet processing as Network.
AC:L - sctp_verify_reconf() allows two RESET_RESPONSE parameters in one chunk, so a peer can send two DENIED responses for the same ADD_OUT request_seq and reliably double-subtract outcnt; RECONF/add-streams being enabled is a deployment condition, not an uncontrolled race.
PR:N - The SCTP handshake and RECONF path require no credentials; AUTH is off by default and RECONF is not AUTH-gated, so any unauthenticated peer of a reachable association can send the triggering chunk.
UI:N - No victim user action is required; duplicate RECONF responses are processed automatically in ESTABLISHED/SHUTDOWN_PENDING once the association has an outstanding multi-parameter ADD_STREAMS request.
S:U - The oops and stream-count corruption stay inside the host kernel SCTP stack and do not cross a VM, IOMMU, or other security-authority boundary.
C:N - SCTP_SO() is genradix_ptr() and returns NULL past preallocated stream slots, so the underflow produces a NULL dereference rather than an out-of-bounds read or kernel memory disclosure.
I:N - The double rollback corrupts the stream count then NULL-dereferences; ext pointers are cleared after kfree, so this is not a use-after-free write primitive or control-flow hijack.
A:H - A wrapped outcnt makes sctp_stream_free(), sendmsg, and other walkers dereference NULL SCTP_SO() slots, causing a kernel oops; extra-shrinking live streams also fails in-flight data, and the peer can abort to force teardown.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: fix stream->outcnt underflow on duplicate RECONF responses

A cached RECONF chunk may contain more than one request parameter.  A
duplicate response can therefore find and process the same ADD_OUT request
again while another parameter is still outstanding, rolling back outcnt
twice and possibly underflowing it.

Track outstanding request types as bits and clear each bit after its first
response.  Later responses for the same request are then ignored.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in the Dynamic Client Registration service of Keycloak, an open-source identity and access management solution. The issue occurs when a user with the view-clients role accesses the client registration endpoint to retrieve client details. Due to a failure to mask sensitive information, the service returns the client's confidential secret in cleartext. cna.title: sunrpc: defer rq_argp and rq_resp free until after RCU grace period

scenarios.value:
AV:L - The use-after-free is reached by NFSD_CMD_RPC_STATUS_GET, a generic-netlink dump over AF_NETLINK that walks svc_rqst threads and reads rq_argp; remote NFS RPCs never enter nfsd_nl_rpc_status_get_dumpit().
AC:L - The attacker fully controls the dumpit reader and can loop it while nfsd threads exit (dynamic idle-timeout kills or thread-count changes), and can further churn threads with NFS traffic; this is an attacker-driven RCU race, not a condition beyond their control.
PR:L - NFSD_CMD_RPC_STATUS_GET is registered with GENL_CMD_CAP_DUMP and no GENL_ADMIN_PERM, so any unprivileged process in the nfsd network namespace can invoke the dump; exploiting it does not require CAP_NET_ADMIN or root.
UI:N - The attacker issues the netlink dump themselves; no separate victim action such as mounting a filesystem or opening a device is required.
S:U - This is a kernel-heap use-after-free in sunrpc/nfsd on the local host; impact stays inside the kernel's security authority and does not cross a VM, IOMMU, or other security boundary.
C:H - dumpit dereferences the kfree'd rq_argp (nfsd4_compoundargs) and reads opcnt/opnums under rcu_read_lock; a kernel UAF with heap reuse of that object yields an arbitrary read primitive.
I:H - The same slab UAF is heap-sprayable so a replaced rq_argp can make dumpit walk attacker-controlled args->ops[], enabling kernel memory corruption and control-flow hijacking.
A:H - Use-after-free of rq_argp while an RCU reader still holds the svc_rqst from sp_all_threads can oops or panic the kernel even if the UAF is not fully turned into code execution.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sunrpc: defer rq_argp and rq_resp free until after RCU grace period

svc_rqst_free() frees rqstp->rq_argp and rqstp->rq_resp synchronously
via kfree(), but defers the rqstp struct free via kfree_rcu().  After
svc_exit_thread() calls list_del_rcu() and svc_rqst_free(), there is
a window where RCU readers that started before list_del_rcu() can still
traverse the thread list and find the rqstp.  These readers (e.g.
nfsd_nl_rpc_status_get_dumpit()) dereference rqstp->rq_argp, which has
already been freed — a use-after-free.

Fix this by moving the kfree of rq_argp and rq_resp into an explicit
call_rcu() callback alongside the struct free.  Resources not accessed
by RCU readers (bvec, buffer pages, scratch folio, auth_data) remain
synchronously freed.

cna.title: @fastify/express vulnerable to path-scoped middleware bypass via absolute-form request targets

descriptions.value: @fastify/express is a Fastify plugin that runs Express middleware inside Fastify. In versions 4.0.5 through 4.0.8, when Fastify runs with the non-default ignoreDuplicateSlashes option enabled, the plugin matches path-scoped Express middleware against a URL whose duplicate-slash normalization has also collapsed the separator after an absolute-form request target's scheme, so Fastify's router resolves the request to the scoped path and runs the handler while the Express layer no longer sees that path. As a result, a request using an absolute-form target can reach a handler on a scoped route such as an admin path while the middleware for authentication, authorization, or rate limiting is skipped. An unauthenticated attacker needs only the non-default ignoreDuplicateSlashes option to be enabled. The issue is fixed in @fastify/express 4.0.9, and users should upgrade to 4.0.9 or later. As a workaround, enforce authentication in a Fastify hook such as preHandler that runs after the router resolves the request, or leave ignoreDuplicateSlashes at its default.

cna.title: Vite: First 4 bytes of files outside of `server.fs` setting is exposed by `?vite-wasm-instance`

descriptions.value: Vite is a frontend tooling framework for JavaScript. From 8.2.0 until 8.2.4 and 8.3.3, the first 4 bytes of files outside of server.fs setting can be returned to the browser by a request containing ?vite-wasm-instance. Requests containing the ?vite-wasm-instance query are handled by the internal Wasm plugin's load hook. The hook removes the query and reads the resulting path directly from disk, but the server.fs checks were not applied. After reading the file, Vite attempts to parse it as WebAssembly. When that parse fails, Node and deno throws an error that contains the first 4 bytes of the file. This vulnerability is fixed in 8.2.4 and 8.3.3.

cna.title: MISP Incomplete Event Deletion Leaves Orphaned Sensitive Records

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [event] Remove every row belonging to an event when

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [event] Remove every row belonging to an event when
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The event deletion routine was extended to cascade-remove all associated child records that were previously left behind. Specifically, the fix ensures that event report tags, event graph rows, shadow attribute correlation rows (on both event_id and 1_event_id foreign keys), fuzzy ssdeep chunks, and attachment scan results are all purged within the same transaction as the parent event deletion, eliminating the orphaned-data condition.
assumptions: The affected version boundary is inferred from the tag_version_boundary metadata (v2.5.48 with 33 commits after fix); the exact fixed release version is not specified in the patch.

The CAPEC-126 mapping is the closest available match; the vulnerability is fundamentally an incomplete cleanup defect rather than a classic state-transition exploit, so the mapping carries uncertainty.

The confidentiality impact is assessed as None because the patch does not demonstrate that orphaned records are accessible to unauthorized users; the primary concern is data integrity and retention policy.
The commit message states the issue was 'found during the internal review, not externally reported,' so no external finder or reporter is credited.
The CVSS assumes the orphaned data is not directly queryable by other users through existing MISP endpoints; if such access paths exist, the confidentiality impact could be higher.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/Model/Event.php, the quickDelete method was modified to: (1) add event_graph and shadow_attribute_correlations (both event_id and 1_event_id) to the relations array used for raw DELETE statements; (2) before executing the raw deletes, query for the IDs of event reports and for attribute/shadow-attribute IDs of type 'attachment' or 'malware-sample'; (3) delete EventReportTag rows matching those report IDs; (4) delete AttachmentScan rows matching those attribute IDs; (5) invoke FuzzyCorrelateSsdeep::purge() to remove ssdeep chunks for the event. All operations occur within the existing database transaction.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: The vulnerability is in a web-based application (AV:N) and requires a straightforward authenticated action (AC:L, AT:N). Deleting events requires elevated privileges (PR:H). No user interaction is needed (UI:N). The primary impact is on the integrity of the vulnerable system's data store: orphaned records persist that should have been removed (VI:L). There is no direct confidentiality impact on the vulnerable system itself because the data was already accessible to the deleting user, and no evidence shows the orphans are exposed to other users (VC:N). No availability impact is demonstrated (VA:N). No impact on subsequent systems (SC:N, SI:N, SA:N).

capecRationale.rationale: The event object transitions to a 'deleted' state, but related child objects (report tags, correlations, scan results, ssdeep chunks) do not follow the expected state transition and remain in an active/persisted state. An attacker with delete privileges could exploit this by creating events with sensitive associated data, deleting the event, and then attempting to access the orphaned records through other application endpoints. This is the closest CAPEC to the observed incomplete state propagation; the mapping is uncertain because the primary issue is a maintenance/cleanup defect rather than a directly exploitable state machine flaw.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The event deletion logic failed to remove all associated child records (report tags, graphs, correlations, ssdeep chunks, scan results), leaving them as orphans in the database. This is a textbook incomplete cleanup of related resources when a parent object is destroyed.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a data integrity flaw in its event deletion logic. When a user deletes an event, several associated records are not removed from the database, leaving them as orphaned entries. The affected record types include event report tags, event graph entries, proposal (shadow attribute) correlations, fuzzy ssdeep correlation chunks, and attachment scan results.

These orphaned records may contain sensitive threat intelligence data such as correlation mappings, scan results, and report metadata that should have been removed along with the parent event. Their persistence beyond the intended deletion lifecycle creates a risk of unintended data retention and potential information exposure if the records are reachable through other application queries or administrative interfaces.

Preconditions:

- An authenticated user with sufficient privileges to delete events in MISP.

- The event must have associated reports, graphs, correlations, ssdeep chunks, or attachment scan results.

Impact:

- Residual sensitive data persists in the database after the parent event is deleted.

- Accumulation of orphaned records over time may contribute to storage bloat.

- Orphaned records may be inadvertently exposed through other data-access paths that do not validate the existence of the parent event.

Affected versions: <2.5.48

cna.title: Pillow: NULL pointer dereference in Image.merge via an unvalidated band 0

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 12.0.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow's Image.merge() can dereference a null image8 plane. Validation skips the first input band, allowing a 32-bit integer or floating-point image backed by image32 storage to be merged as a narrower multiband image. A crafted IPTC file can reach this path when an application opens and loads it, or a caller can invoke Image.merge() directly with such a first band. This causes a native process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

cna.title: Pillow: TIFF encoder ColorMap plane-size mismatch causes a heap out-of-bounds read

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's TIFF encoder can read beyond a ColorMap buffer when retained TIFF metadata has a plane size inconsistent with BitsPerSample. A small TIFF can be opened normally and then retain a crafted ColorMap that is reused when the image is saved. An application that re-encodes the attacker's TIFF with libtiff can trigger the out-of-bounds read. This can disclose heap memory in the output or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

cna.title: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in ImagingJpegDecode

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's JPEG decoder can write a full-width scanline into a buffer sized for a requested draft scale. ImagingJpegDecode does not verify libjpeg's actual output width and component count after scaling is requested, and an 8-bit lossless SOF3 JPEG decoded by a build linked to libjpeg-turbo 3.x can ignore the requested downscaling geometry. An attacker can supply such a JPEG to an application that uses draft() or thumbnail() to request downscaling. This can corrupt heap memory, crash the process, or potentially allow code execution. cna.title: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIO

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 2.0.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow has a heap buffer overflow and stale-heap disclosure in _tiffWriteProc when saving compressed TIFF data through libtiff to a target without a usable fileno(), such as BytesIO. The callback sizes its allocation from the prior buffer size instead of the current write position, allowing an attacker-controlled out-of-line TIFF tag or retained ICC profile to be copied beyond the allocation after libtiff seeks forward. This overflow can crash the process and may allow code execution. Independently, unwritten alignment gaps in compressed TIFF output larger than 64 KiB can disclose stale heap bytes without a crafted tag. File paths and targets with real file descriptors are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

cna.title: MISP Proposal ACL Bypass: Incomplete Distribution Level Check in Shadow Attribute Access Control

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [proposals] Apply the attribute ACL rules to proposals

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [proposals] Apply the attribute ACL rules to proposals
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix enforces the distribution level constraint in the sharing group access check, requiring distribution level 4 (All communities) for the sharing group test to apply. Additionally, the owning organisation is now explicitly granted access to proposals on its own attributes regardless of distribution level, correcting the over-restrictive behavior.
assumptions: The CAPEC mapping (CAPEC-2, Parameter Tampering) is the closest available match but is uncertain; the vulnerability is more accurately a missing authorization check (incomplete ACL evaluation) rather than active parameter manipulation by the attacker.
The affected version boundary is inferred from the tag v2.5.48 and the commit position (35 commits after the fix); exact version boundaries are not explicitly stated in the patch metadata.

The second aspect of the vulnerability (owner organisation denied access to its own proposals) is primarily a functional/availability defect rather than a security vulnerability, but is included as part of the same fix and the same root cause (incomplete ACL logic).
CVSS PR:L assumes the attacker must be an authenticated MISP user with membership in a relevant sharing group; no evidence supports unauthenticated access.
The Co-Authored-By line credits an AI assistant (Claude Opus 5.5) as a remediation developer; this is recorded as-is from the commit metadata.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In the shadow attribute model's condition builder, the sharing group check for both objects and attributes now includes an AND condition requiring distribution = 4 alongside the sharing_group_id IN check. The attribute distribution condition was changed from a simple sharing_group_id IN clause to a compound AND condition with distribution = 4. A new OR condition (Event.org_id matching the user's org_id) was added to grant the owning organisation access to proposals on its own attributes.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: MISP is a network-accessible web application. AC:L: The user only needs to be a member of a sharing group; no special conditions or race conditions are required. AT:N: No active attack requirements beyond normal API usage. PR:L: The attacker must be an authenticated user with membership in a relevant sharing group. UI:N: No user interaction is required; the check is server-side. VC:H: The user can view proposals (proposed attribute changes) that should be restricted by distribution level, disclosing sensitive information about proposed changes. VI:N: No integrity impact; the user cannot modify proposals. VA:N: No availability impact. SC/SI/SA:N: No impact on subsequent components.

capecRationale.rationale: The user's sharing group membership (a parameter of their identity/session) was leveraged by the flawed authorization logic to grant access to proposals without the required distribution level check. This is the closest available CAPEC pattern; the user is not actively tampering with parameters, but the system improperly treats group membership as a sufficient access parameter without enforcing the additional distribution constraint. The mapping is uncertain because the vulnerability is more accurately a missing authorization check than active parameter manipulation.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The authorization check for proposal visibility was missing the distribution level constraint. The system evaluated sharing group membership as sufficient for access without also requiring the distribution level to be 4 (All communities), resulting in an incomplete authorization check that allowed access to proposals on more restrictively distributed attributes.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains an access control flaw in the proposal (shadow attribute) visibility logic. The authorization check accepted any attribute or object carrying one of the user's sharing groups without verifying the distribution level, and denied the owning organisation access to proposals on its own organisation-only attributes.

- A user belonging to a sharing group could view proposals on attributes or objects with that sharing group, regardless of the attribute's distribution level (levels 1-3 should restrict visibility)

- The owning organisation could not view proposals on its own org-only attributes

Security impact: Unauthorized disclosure of proposed attribute changes to users who should not have access based on distribution level restrictions.

Affected: <2.5.48

ai_annotations.description: Draft vulnerability metadata was generated from a git-format patch using an Ollama-hosted language model. Human validation is required before publication.

patches.subject: fix: [workflows] Escape misp-module parameter names used as

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [workflows] Escape misp-module parameter names used as
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix applies HTML output encoding (the h() helper) to the parameter name before it is used as a form label, ensuring that any HTML metacharacters in the value are neutralized and rendered as inert text rather than executable markup.
assumptions: The misp-modules service is assumed to be a component whose output can be influenced by a module developer or a compromised service endpoint; the exact attack vector for injecting a malicious parameter name is not detailed in the patch.
MISP requires authentication to access the workflow module page; PR:L is assumed based on MISP's standard access model.
The affected version boundary (< 2.5.48) is inferred from the tag_version_boundary metadata (v2.5.48, 25 commits after fix); the exact first affected version is not specified.
CAPEC-1 (Reflected XSS) is the closest match; the data source is a backend service rather than a direct request parameter, but the unencoded reflection into HTML is the defining characteristic.
The h() function is assumed to be CakePHP's HTML-encoding helper (equivalent to htmlspecialchars), based on the framework context of the MISP codebase.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/Model/WorkflowModules/Module_misp_module.php, the translateParams method was modified: the 'label' array element changed from Inflector::humanize($paramName) to h(Inflector::humanize($paramName)), wrapping the humanized parameter name in CakePHP's HTML-encoding function before it is assigned as a form label.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N – web-based, reachable over the network. AC:L – no race or special timing; the misp-modules service simply needs to return a crafted parameter name. AT:N – no manipulation of the target system required. PR:L – the victim must be an authenticated MISP user to view the workflow module page. UI:A – the victim must actively load the workflow module page for the script to execute. VC/VI/VA:N – the MISP server itself is not compromised. SC:L – the attacker can read cookies or session data in the victim's browser. SI:L – the attacker can modify the page or perform actions in the victim's session. SA:N – no elevation of security authority on the server.

capecRationale.rationale: The misp-modules service supplies parameter names that are reflected into the HTML of the workflow module page without encoding. The attacker-controlled data flows from an external source into the rendered output, matching the reflected XSS pattern. Uncertainty: the data originates from a backend service rather than a direct HTTP parameter, but the effect (untrusted data reflected into HTML without encoding) is functionally identical to reflected XSS.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The parameter name from an external service is inserted into HTML output (a form label) without HTML encoding, allowing injected markup or script to execute in the victim's browser. This is a textbook reflected XSS.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a reflected cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the workflow module interface. Parameter names returned by the misp-modules service are rendered as raw HTML form labels on the workflow module page without output encoding. An attacker who can influence the parameter names reported by the misp-modules service can inject arbitrary HTML or JavaScript that executes in the context of an authenticated MISP user's browser.

Preconditions:

- The attacker must be able to control or influence parameter names reported by the misp-modules service.

- A victim must be authenticated and view the affected workflow module page.

Impact:

- Execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser session.

- Potential theft of session tokens, manipulation of the MISP interface, or initiation of unauthorized actions on behalf of the victim.

Affected versions: <2.5.48.

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 8.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow's TIFF tile and RGBA decode paths can read beyond row data produced by libtiff. In _decodeTile and the RGBA unpacker path, when Pillow and libtiff interpret duplicated PhotometricInterpretation or BitsPerSample tags differently, Pillow does not verify that the required input row fits inside the row libtiff produced, while the strip path has this validation. Loading pixels from such a crafted TIFF can expose adjacent heap data in output pixels or crash the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

cna.title: Robots::Validate versions from 0.4.3 before 0.4.10 for Perl report clients as imposter robots when User-Agent matcher state carries over from a previous request

solutions.value:
Upgrade to Robots-Validate v0.4.10 or later.

Deployments with Algorithm::AhoCorasick::XS should upgrade to v0.4.11, which fixed a bug with using that version.

descriptions.value:
Robots::Validate versions from 0.4.3 before 0.4.10 for Perl report clients as imposter robots when User-Agent matcher state carries over from a previous request.

Each Robots::Validate object holds one pure-Perl Aho-Corasick search machine and feeds every User-Agent into it without resetting its state. A User-Agent that ends part-way through a robot name leaves the machine mid-match, so the next User-Agent checked by the same object can complete that name. That client's address is then checked against the robot's DNS rule, which it fails.

A remote client can use this to make a site that blocks bad robots block other visitors where the prefix User-Agent string is a suffix of a robot being validated.

Note that deployments with Algorithm::AhoCorasick::XS are also affected, since it was unused due to a different bug.

cna.title: webpack-dev-server vulnerable to cross-origin WebSocket access via proxied upgrades

descriptions.value: webpack-dev-server is a development server that provides live reloading for webpack projects. In versions before 5.2.7 and in version 6.0.0, when a proxy entry is configured to forward WebSockets, the server forwards non-HMR WebSocket upgrade requests to the proxy target without validating the Host or Origin headers, so the allowedHosts protection does not apply to those proxied upgrades. A malicious web page visited by a developer can open a cross-origin WebSocket through the dev server and read from and write to the proxied backend, even when the server is bound to loopback. The issue is fixed in webpack-dev-server 5.2.7 and 6.1.0, where proxied WebSocket upgrades pass the same Host and Origin validation as the HMR WebSocket, and users should upgrade to one of those versions or later. As a workaround, omit WebSocket forwarding from proxy entries that do not need it and scope the proxy to specific paths.

x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix introduces strict validation of the tag colour value before it is rendered into a CSS style attribute. Only values matching a valid six-digit hexadecimal colour pattern (e.g. #aabbcc) are accepted; any other value is replaced with a safe default (#ffffff). This prevents arbitrary CSS from being injected through the colour field, aligning the remote tag handling with the validation already applied to local tags.
assumptions: The affected version boundary is inferred from the tag_version_boundary metadata (v2.5.48, 27 commits after fix); the exact first affected version is not stated in the patch.
PR:L assumes that creating or modifying a tag on a linked MISP server requires only low-level user privileges; the exact permission model was not verified from the patch.
SC:L assumes CSS injection could enable limited client-side information disclosure (e.g., via CSS selectors or layout manipulation); full XSS or data exfiltration is not evidenced.
CAPEC-66 is the closest available mapping; no CAPEC specifically models CSS injection via trusted inter-instance data, so this mapping carries uncertainty.
The commit message states the issue was found during internal review and not externally reported; no external finder or reporter is credited.
The Co-Authored-By line references an AI tool (Claude Opus 5.5); it is credited as a tool rather than a human remediation developer.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/View/Servers/preview_event.ctp, a regex check (preg_match against /^#[0-9a-f]{6}$/i) is added before the tag colour is used. If the colour does not match the hex pattern, it defaults to #ffffff. The validated $colour variable replaces the raw $tag['colour'] in both the background-color style property and the getTextColour() call, eliminating the untrusted value from the CSS context.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N – the attack originates from a remote linked MISP server over the network. AC:L – no race conditions or special timing; simply setting a tag colour suffices. AT:N – no manipulation of the attack target is required. PR:L – the attacker needs low-privilege access (tag creation) on the linked server. UI:A – the victim must actively navigate to the event preview page. VC:N – no direct confidentiality loss on the vulnerable system. VI:N – no integrity impact on the vulnerable system's data. VA:N – no availability impact. SC:L – CSS injection may allow limited information disclosure on the client (e.g., reading page structure via CSS selectors or side channels). SI:L – the attacker can modify the visual presentation of the preview page (UI manipulation, overlay, spoofing). SA:N – no security authority impact.

capecRationale.rationale: The attack exploits the inherent trust between linked MISP instances. The local instance accepts and renders data (tag colours) from a remote linked server without sufficient validation, assuming the data is well-formed. The attacker leverages this trusted relationship to inject CSS. This is the closest CAPEC; no CAPEC specifically models CSS injection via trusted data sources, so CAPEC-66 is the best available match.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a CSS injection vulnerability in the remote event preview feature. When a user previews an event from a linked MISP server, the colour value associated with each remote tag is written directly into an inline CSS style attribute without sufficient validation. Although HTML entity encoding is applied, the value is interpreted as CSS within the style attribute, allowing a malicious or compromised linked server to inject arbitrary CSS declarations.

An attacker with the ability to create or modify tags on a linked MISP instance can craft a tag colour value containing CSS injection payloads. When a user on the local instance views the event preview, the injected CSS is rendered, potentially allowing UI manipulation, visual spoofing, or limited information disclosure through CSS-based techniques.

Preconditions:

- A linked MISP server relationship exists between the victim instance and the attacker-controlled instance.

- The attacker can create or modify tags on the linked server.

- A victim user views the remote event preview page.

Affected: <2.5.48.

x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The fix ensures that the redacted and cli_only flags declared by a module in its own setting definition are preserved when the server rebuilds the setting for API exposure. By carrying these flags through to the final setting object, the existing enforcement logic (which checks these flags before serving values or accepting edits) now correctly applies to module-supplied settings, preventing disclosure of redacted values and blocking API-based modification of CLI-only settings.
assumptions: The affected version boundary is inferred from the tag_version_boundary metadata (fix is 10 commits after v2.5.48); the exact fixed release version is not stated in the patch metadata.
PR:L assumes that reading server settings requires an authenticated MISP user with appropriate role permissions; the patch does not specify the exact permission level required.

The CAPEC-126 mapping is the closest available pattern for the information-disclosure aspect; the authorization-bypass aspect (cli_only) does not have a precise CAPEC match and is subsumed under the same mapping.
VC:L assumes the exposed data is limited to module-specific API keys rather than system-wide credentials; the actual sensitivity depends on which modules are installed.

The commit message references a separate issue (branch read) reported by Jeroen Pinoy; this vulnerability was discovered as a side effect of fixing that issue, so Jeroen Pinoy is not credited as a finder of this specific vulnerability.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/Model/Server.php, within the readModuleSettings() method, a loop was added after the setting fields are populated that iterates over the strings 'redacted' and 'cli_only'. For each flag, if the module's own result array contains a truthy value for that key, the flag is set to true on the rebuilt $setting object before it is stored in $serverSettings. This is a 6-line addition that preserves the module-declared guard flags that were previously discarded during the setting reconstruction.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: MISP is a web application accessible over the network. AC:L: No special race conditions or complex setup are needed; a standard API call to the settings endpoint triggers the issue. AT:N: No manipulation of the attack target is required. PR:L: The attacker needs an authenticated MISP account with permission to view server settings. UI:N: No user interaction is required. VC:L: Sensitive module API keys are exposed, but the scope is limited to settings of modules that declare the redacted flag. VI:N: No direct integrity impact on the vulnerable component's data beyond the VA impact. VA:L: CLI-only settings can be modified via the API, representing a limited integrity impact on the vulnerable component's configuration. SC/SI/SA:N: No evidence of impact on other components or systems.

capecRationale.rationale: The primary impact is that sensitive data (module API keys marked as redacted) is discoverable via standard API endpoints because the redaction flag was not enforced. An authenticated user querying server settings can obtain credentials that the module author intended to keep hidden. This is the closest CAPEC to the information-disclosure aspect of the vulnerability. The secondary aspect (CLI-only settings editable via API) is an authorization bypass that does not map cleanly to a single CAPEC; CAPEC-126 is selected as the best available match for the overall pattern of accessing data that should be restricted.

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: The redacted flag, which instructs the server to mask a setting's value (e.g., an API key), was dropped during setting reconstruction. This caused the sensitive value to be served in plaintext via API endpoints to any authenticated user, constituting an information exposure.

The cli_only flag, which restricts a setting to command-line modification only, was dropped during setting reconstruction. This allowed the setting to be modified via the web API without the intended authorization restriction, effectively bypassing the access control the module author specified.

descriptions.value:
MISP contains a vulnerability in the handling of module plugin settings. When the server rebuilds module-supplied settings for API consumption, it drops the redacted and cli_only flags that a module declares in its own configuration metadata.

As a result:

- A module that marks a setting (such as an API key) as redacted still has its value returned in full by the servers/getSetting and servers/serverSettingsEdit endpoints, exposing sensitive credentials to any authenticated user who can read server settings.

- A module that marks a setting as cli_only (intended to be editable only via the command-line interface) can still be modified through the web API, bypassing the intended access restriction.

An authenticated user with access to server settings can therefore read sensitive module credentials and modify settings that the module author intended to restrict to CLI-only access.

Affected: <2.5.48

cna.title: Pillow: Quadratic GIF comment copying during save

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 9.2.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow performs quadratic copying when saving a GIF with a long comment. _get_global_header() repeatedly copies portions of comment data while assembling the global header, including comments retained from an untrusted input image. An attacker can supply an image with a large GIF comment to an application that saves it as GIF. This can consume excessive CPU and delay or deny service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: Traefik before 2.11.46, 3.6.17, and 3.7.1 Cross-Namespace Resource Reference via Kubernetes Annotations

descriptions.value: Traefik before 2.11.46, 3.x before 3.6.17, and 3.7.0 lack namespace validation for Ingress and Service annotations in the Kubernetes Ingress provider, allowing references to Middlewares, ServersTransports, and TLSOptions in other namespaces. Attackers able to create or update Ingress or Service resources in one namespace can set router.middlewares or service.serverstransport annotations to obtain another tenant's injected credentials or reuse its client certificates, bypassing namespace-based tenant isolation.

cna.title: Tandoor Recipes < 2.7.0 Cross-Space Permission Cache Poisoning

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: Tandoor Recipes < 2.7.0 Cross-Space Permission Cache Poisoning

descriptions.value: Tandoor Recipes before 2.7.0 contains an improper cache-key design in cookbook/helper/permission_helper.py that allows authenticated users to retain stale group-based permissions across different spaces by exploiting a cache key keyed only on user id while omitting the active space, with the cached entry's TTL refreshed on every request. Attackers can create their own space to obtain an admin group designation, then switch their active space to a victim space where they hold lesser privileges, causing the stale cached admin decision to authorize elevated access and bypass group revocations or demotions across multiple permission classes and views.

cna.title: launch-editor: Editor CLI flag misinterpretation causing arbitrary command execution for some editors

descriptions.value: launch-editor allows users to open files with line numbers in editor from Node.js. Prior to 2.14.2, when an attacker can create a filesystem entry beginning with plus or minus in the working directory, an affected editor is selected, and the path can remain relative or is converted to a relative WSL path, launchEditor forwards the path without forcing it to be interpreted as a positional filename. Editor option parsing then treats the attacker-controlled filename as a command-line flag, which can cause unintended file overwrite or arbitrary command execution by the selected editor. The affected editors are Vim and gVim, MacVim, Emacs and Emacsclient, and Notepad++ when a plugin exposes dangerous operations; WSL path conversion keeps Vite and newer middleware callers exposed. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.2.

descriptions.value: ApostropheCMS is an open-source Node.js content management system. Prior to 3.7.1 of the import-export module, predictable export archive filenames allow an unauthenticated requester to download another user's export from publicly readable export storage before the archive expires or is removed. A user with export permission must first create the archive, and sites with exports disabled, private upload storage, or authenticated upload delivery are not exposed through this network-download path. This issue is fixed in version 3.7.1.

cna.title: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in FlashPix (FPX) JPEG decoding leads to code execution

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, Pillow's FlashPix JPEG-tile decoder can write decoded scanlines beyond the allocated tile buffer. FlashPix (FPX) JPEG decoding selects raw mode LA with two bytes per pixel, while an unrecognized JPEG mode can be decoded as JCS_UNKNOWN with four components, causing ImagingJpegDecode to write four-component scanlines into the two-byte tile buffer. An attacker can supply a crafted OLE2 FlashPix file to an application with the optional olefile dependency installed that opens or thumbnails untrusted input. This can corrupt heap memory and may allow arbitrary code execution. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

patches.subject: fix: [sync] Filter the tags of every event report pushed to a

x_patch2vuln.subject: fix: [sync] Filter the tags of every event report pushed to a
x_patch2vuln.fixSummary: The non-exportable tag filtering is now invoked for each individual event report within the iteration loop, ensuring that restricted tags are removed from every report before it is transmitted to the remote MISP instance. This prevents the leakage of tags that were explicitly marked as non-exportable.
assumptions: The affected version boundary is inferred from the tag_version_boundary metadata (v2.5.48 with 34 commits after fix), suggesting the fix is included in v2.5.48 and prior versions are affected. No explicit version range is stated in the patch.
PR:L assumes that a non-admin authenticated user with push-to-remote permissions can trigger the sync; if only administrators can initiate sync, PR should be raised to H.
The CAPEC-128 mapping is uncertain; no CAPEC pattern precisely describes a per-item filtering logic error causing data leakage during a legitimate operation.
The security impact is assessed as limited to tag disclosure; the actual sensitivity of 'non-exportable' tags depends on MISP deployment configuration and is not specified in the patch.
The availability impact (null report push causing remote save failure) is considered minor and not reflected in the CVSS vector as the primary concern is information disclosure.
x_patch2vuln.patchSummary: In app/Model/Event.php, the call to __removeNonExportableTags was moved from a single post-loop invocation (which used the last $key value from the foreach) into the else branch of the loop body, so it executes for each non-empty report individually. The post-loop else block that applied the filter to a single report was removed, eliminating both the tag-leakage bug and the null-report push when the last report was empty.
x_patch2vuln.cvssRationale: AV:N: The vulnerability is triggered over the network during MISP-to-MISP synchronization. AC:L: No special conditions are needed beyond a configured sync relationship and an event with multiple reports. AT:N: No attacker interaction is required; the bug triggers on any sync push. PR:L: An authenticated user with permission to push events to a remote server is required. UI:N: No user interaction beyond initiating the sync. VC:L: Non-exportable tags (restricted metadata) are disclosed to the remote instance; the core event data is not exposed. VI:N, VA:N: No integrity or availability impact on the local instance. SC:N, SI:N, SA:N: No impact on the remote instance's confidentiality, integrity, or availability beyond receiving the tags it should not have.

capecRationale.rationale: This is the closest available CAPEC pattern. The vulnerability arises from a code logic error that causes data (non-exportable tags) to be improperly exposed during a legitimate sync operation. The mapping is uncertain because the issue is a logic bug in data filtering rather than a deliberate attacker action; no CAPEC pattern precisely covers 'improper per-item filtering in a loop causing data leakage during a legitimate API operation.'

modelComparison.selectionNotice: The selected result is closest to model consensus; this heuristic does not establish factual correctness and human review remains required.

weaknessRationale.rationale: Tags explicitly marked as non-exportable were not filtered from event reports during synchronization, exposing restricted information to the remote MISP instance. The root cause is a logic error (filter applied once instead of per-item), but the security consequence is information disclosure.

descriptions.value:
In MISP, the event synchronization process contained a logic error in the preparation of event reports for remote push. The filtering of non-exportable tags was applied only once after the iteration over all reports, rather than to each individual report.

As a result:

- All reports except the last one in the set were pushed to the remote MISP instance with their non-exportable tags intact, effectively disclosing restricted tag information to the receiving instance.

- When the last report in the set was withheld (empty), a null report was pushed, causing the remote instance to fail saving the event.

This issue affects any MISP instance configured to push events with multiple reports to a remote server via synchronization.

Affected: <2.5.48.

cna.title: Pillow: TiffDecode returns uninitialized memory as pixels for short JPEG strips

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.3.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can return uninitialized memory as pixels when libtiff performs a short decode of JPEG-compressed or Group 4 fax TIFF data. The _decodeStrip and _decodeTile buffers can be larger than the bytes written by libtiff, but Pillow converts the expected rows without clearing the unwritten tail. The tile path is affected from 5.3.0 and the strip path from 6.0.0. An attacker can supply a crafted TIFF to an application that loads and returns or re-encodes its pixels. This can disclose stale heap contents without memory corruption or a process crash. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

From 3.32.6 until 4.2.1, SoftFileLock can follow a swapped symbolic link during the conditional os.access writability check for a node without its owner-write bit, allowing another local user on a platform and directory configuration that follows the link to infer whether a chosen path exists and is writable from the observable acquisition result. This issue is fixed in version 4.2.1.

solutions.value: Apply upstream commit 7cf75587b6f38b87849fe192bf5dfd124b7702bc or a verified branch-specific backport. The fix requires the original IPv6 destination-prefix component to have offset zero before it can pass FlowSpec validation. The first fixed release has not yet been verified.

supportingMedia.value: Apply upstream commit 7cf75587b6f38b87849fe192bf5dfd124b7702bc or a verified branch-specific backport. The fix requires the original IPv6 destination-prefix component to have offset zero before it can pass FlowSpec validation. The first fixed release has not yet been verified.

descriptions.value: An IPv6 FlowSpec validation bypass in the CZ.NIC BIRD Internet Routing Daemon allows an established BGP peer to inject FlowSpec rules matching destinations outside the address space authorized by the unicast-route validation procedure. With validation enabled on the receiving flow6 channel, BIRD fails to reject a destination prefix component with a nonzero offset, contrary to RFC 8956 section 5. It validates a reconstructed prefix with zero-filled skipped bits, although the original FlowSpec component can match a broader set of IPv6 addresses. Given a suitable unicast route from the peer, the rule can pass validation and, where export policy permits, be propagated to downstream peers. Downstream enforcement may cause unauthorized traffic filtering or redirection.

descriptions.description: CWE-1284 Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input

configurations.value: An established BGP peer must be able to send IPv6 FlowSpec to a receiving flow6 channel configured with "validate yes". A suitable unicast route from that peer must be present in the base table. Propagation additionally requires an export policy permitting the rule. Data-plane impact depends on downstream support for, acceptance of, and enforcement of the FlowSpec match and action.

supportingMedia.value: An established BGP peer must be able to send IPv6 FlowSpec to a receiving flow6 channel configured with "validate yes". A suitable unicast route from that peer must be present in the base table. Propagation additionally requires an export policy permitting the rule. cna.title: Pillow: Quadratic GIF comment concatenation allows DoS in Image.open()

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.4.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow performs quadratic copying while parsing GIF comments. GifImageFile._seek() repeatedly appends immutable bytes for comment sub-blocks and multiple comment extensions, and frame zero is parsed during Image.open(). An attacker can submit a small-dimension GIF containing many comment extensions to any application that opens the file. This can consume excessive CPU and deny service before the application can inspect the image. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

descriptions.value: The Bootstrap Shortcodes plugin for WordPress before 3.4.6 is vulnerable to stored XSS via the id attribute of the [bs_tcontent] shortcode. The bs_tcontent() shortcode handler in inc/bs_tabs.php emits the id attribute value into an unquoted HTML attribute. esc_attr() is applied, but it does not encode space characters, so a space in the supplied value terminates the attribute and any following text is parsed as additional HTML attributes, including JavaScript event handlers. cna.title: Pillow: APNG background disposal allocates full canvas before decompression bomb check

descriptions.value: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 8.1.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow can allocate an APNG disposal background at the full canvas size before applying the decompression-bomb check. A crafted APNG with a small first frame, a very large declared canvas, and background disposal or first-frame OP_PREVIOUS reaches PngImageFile._seek while Image.open() positions frame zero. The full-canvas allocation occurs inside Image.open() without requiring pixel loading or frame iteration. This can exhaust memory and deny service. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

cna.title: Vitest: Windows backslash traversal bypasses the @vitest/mocker redirect allowlist fix

descriptions.value: Vitest is a Vite-native testing framework for JavaScript and TypeScript projects. From 4.1.11 until 4.1.12 and 5.0.3, isFileLoadingAllowed and the filesystem read interpret backslashes differently on Windows in packages/mocker/src/node/interceptorPlugin.ts. When a client can reach the Vite dev server on Windows and register a redirect mock containing backslash traversal, POSIX joining preserves a Windows backslash traversal that the later filesystem read interprets as a path separator, so the client can read a file outside server.fs.allow that the Vitest process can access. solutions.value: Upgrade to P-Net 1.0.3 or later.

supportingMedia.value: Upgrade to P-Net 1.0.3 or later.

descriptions.value: P-Net before 1.0.3 does not release the Application Relationship (AR) and the RPC session when an RPC request is rejected because its data representation has incorrect endianness. The session and its AR remain allocated, so repeated requests exhaust the available sessions. Once they are exhausted the device no longer answers new RPC requests, including Connect, until it is restarted. A remote unauthenticated attacker can use this to cause a denial of service.

cna.title: filelock: ReadWriteLock on Windows acts on SQLite side files another local user places beside its database

descriptions.value: filelock is a platform-independent file lock for Python. From 3.20.4 until 4.2.1, ReadWriteLock and AsyncReadWriteLock on Windows use _connect to attach SQLite to the lock database by pathname, allowing another local account that can create adjacent names to place a database-wal or database-journal side file before acquisition. An undeletable WAL file makes each read or write acquisition fail immediately with sqlite3.OperationalError regardless of timeout. Separately, when the database contains at least one table, a hot journal that grants the lock account modify rights can cause SQLite recovery to delete a file named by that journal only when the lock account has permission to delete the target. The issue requires a directory writable by another account, such as a shared Windows temporary directory, and does not affect private directories. This issue is fixed in version 4.2.1.
A downgrade issue was addressed with additional version checks. This issue is fixed in macOS Golden Gate 27.2, macOS Sequoia 15.8.2, macOS Tahoe 26.7.2. An app may be able to gain root privileges.
