cna.title: xfrm6: fix uninitialized saddr in xfrm6_get_saddr()

scenarios.value:
AV:N - A network-triggered path exists on an IPv6/IPsec endpoint: received IPv6 traffic that causes kernel-generated output, such as ICMPv6/NDISC replies or service responses, enters xfrm_lookup_route() and reaches xfrm_tmpl_resolve_one()->xfrm6_get_saddr(). The same code is locally reachable with sendmsg(), but a reasonably configured XFRM/IPsec host can be triggered by network traffic.
AC:L - No race, heap grooming, or timing condition is required; once the affected outbound XFRM template has a wildcard IPv6 tunnel source and source address selection fails, the unchecked error path is deterministic. Matching output traffic can be triggered repeatedly.
PR:N - The network trigger does not require the attacker to authenticate or hold local privileges. Creating the XFRM policy requires CAP_NET_ADMIN, including via a user/net namespace for local testing, but in the network scenario that policy is preexisting victim configuration.
UI:N - No victim user action is required after the vulnerable XFRM/IPsec configuration is present. Packets or local sends directly drive the kernel output path.
S:U - The bug affects kernel XFRM/IPv6 processing within the same host security authority. It does not cross a VM, IOMMU, or separate security scope boundary.
C:L - The uninitialized value is a bounded 16-byte IPv6 source address from kernel stack, used in hashes/comparisons and potentially copied into XFRM acquire state/messages. This is limited kernel memory disclosure, not an arbitrary read primitive.
I:L - The uninitialized source address can influence XFRM state lookup/acquire behavior and create or notify state using an unintended local tunnel endpoint. This is limited integrity impact to IPsec/XFRM state handling, not arbitrary modification.
A:H - Syzbot reported a kernel BUG/KMSAN finding in xfrm_state_find(), and the bad value is consumed in core XFRM state lookup/acquire paths that can be triggered repeatedly. Kernel warning/oops/panic conditions are high availability impact.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfrm6: fix uninitialized saddr in xfrm6_get_saddr()

xfrm6_get_saddr() does not check the return value of
ipv6_dev_get_saddr(). When ipv6_dev_get_saddr() fails to find a suitable
source address (returns -EADDRNOTAVAIL), saddr->in6 is left
uninitialized, but xfrm6_get_saddr() still returns 0 (success).

This causes the caller xfrm_tmpl_resolve_one() to use the uninitialized
address in xfrm_state_find(), triggering KMSAN warning:

=====================================================
BUG: KMSAN: uninit-value in xfrm_state_find+0x2424/0xa940
 xfrm_state_find+0x2424/0xa940
 xfrm_resolve_and_create_bundle+0x906/0x5a20
 xfrm_lookup_with_ifid+0xcc0/0x3770
 xfrm_lookup_route+0x63/0x2b0
 ip_route_output_flow+0x1ce/0x270
 udp_sendmsg+0x2ce1/0x3400
 inet_sendmsg+0x1ef/0x2a0
 __sock_sendmsg+0x278/0x3d0
 __sys_sendto+0x593/0x720
 __x64_sys_sendto+0x130/0x200

 do_syscall_64+0xd3/0xf80

Local variable tmp.i.i created at:
 xfrm_resolve_and_create_bundle+0x3e3/0x5a20

=====================================================

Fix by checking the return value of ipv6_dev_get_saddr() and propagating
the error.

cna.title: media: v4l2-async: Fix error handling on steps after finding a match

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

media: v4l2-async: Fix error handling on steps after finding a match

Once an async connection is found to be matching with an fwnode, a
sub-device may be registered (in case it wasn't already), its bound
operation is called, ancillary links are created, the async connection
is added to the sub-device's list of connections and removed from the
global waiting connection list. Further on, the sub-device's possible own
notifier is searched for possible additional matches.

Fix these specific issues:

- If v4l2_async_match_notify() failed before the sub-notifier handling,
  the async connection was unbound and its entry removed from the
  sub-device's async connection list. The latter part was also done in
  v4l2_async_match_notify().

- The async connection's sd field was only set after creating ancillary
  links in v4l2_async_match_notify(). It was however dereferenced in
  v4l2_async_unbind_subdev_one(), which was called on error path of
  v4l2_async_match_notify() failure.

cna.title: net: qrtr: replace qrtr_tx_flow radix_tree with xarray to fix memory leak

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: qrtr: replace qrtr_tx_flow radix_tree with xarray to fix memory leak

__radix_tree_create() allocates and links intermediate nodes into the
tree one by one. If a subsequent allocation fails, the already-linked
nodes remain in the tree with no corresponding leaf entry. These orphaned
internal nodes are never reclaimed because radix_tree_for_each_slot()
only visits slots containing leaf values.

The radix_tree API is deprecated in favor of xarray. As suggested by
Matthew Wilcox, migrate qrtr_tx_flow from radix_tree to xarray instead
of fixing the radix_tree itself [1]. xarray properly handles cleanup of
internal nodes — xa_destroy() frees all internal xarray nodes when the
qrtr_node is released, preventing the leak.

[1] https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260225071623.41275-1-jiayuan.chen@linux.dev/T/

cna.title: cpufreq: governor: fix double free in cpufreq_dbs_governor_init() error path

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

cpufreq: governor: fix double free in cpufreq_dbs_governor_init() error path

When kobject_init_and_add() fails, cpufreq_dbs_governor_init() calls
kobject_put(&dbs_data->attr_set.kobj).

The kobject release callback cpufreq_dbs_data_release() calls
gov->exit(dbs_data) and kfree(dbs_data), but the current error path
then calls gov->exit(dbs_data) and kfree(dbs_data) again, causing a
double free.

Keep the direct kfree(dbs_data) for the gov->init() failure path, but
after kobject_init_and_add() has been called, let kobject_put() handle
the cleanup through cpufreq_dbs_data_release().

cna.title: OpenClaw 2026.2.21 < 2026.4.10 - Authentication Bypass in Sandbox noVNC Helper Route

references.name: VulnCheck Advisory: OpenClaw 2026.2.21 < 2026.4.10 - Authentication Bypass in Sandbox noVNC Helper Route

cna.title: net/sched: act_skbedit: fix divide-by-zero in tcf_skbedit_hash()

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/sched: act_skbedit: fix divide-by-zero in tcf_skbedit_hash()

Commit 38a6f0865796 ("net: sched: support hash selecting tx queue")
added SKBEDIT_F_TXQ_SKBHASH support. The inclusive range size is
computed as:

mapping_mod = queue_mapping_max - queue_mapping + 1;

The range size can be 65536 when the requested range covers all possible
u16 queue IDs (e.g. queue_mapping=0 and queue_mapping_max=U16_MAX).
That value cannot be represented in a u16 and previously wrapped to 0,
so tcf_skbedit_hash() could trigger a divide-by-zero:

queue_mapping += skb_get_hash(skb) % params->mapping_mod;

Compute mapping_mod in a wider type and reject ranges larger than U16_MAX
to prevent params->mapping_mod from becoming 0 and avoid the crash.

The most impactful abuse is /Admin/RunSql, whose OnPostRunQuery binds Editor from the POST body and passes it straight to IDbAccess.RunSql with no caller check, yielding arbitrary SQL execution for any low-privileged user. descriptions.value: FOSSBilling is a free, open-source billing and client management system. Prior to version 0.8.0, when a client or staff/admin account is suspended or marked inactive, existing authenticated sessions are not invalidated. The session identity loaders in src/di.php (loggedin_client and loggedin_admin) only reject sessions if the backing account record no longer exists in the database. cna.title: netfilter: ctnetlink: ensure safe access to master conntrack

scenarios.value:
AV:L - The vulnerable ctnetlink expectation operations are reached through NETLINK_NETFILTER messages from local userspace, not directly by remote packets.
AC:L - The race is between attacker-driven ctnetlink expectation lookup/dump/delete and attacker-driven master conntrack deletion or timeout, so the attacker can create and retry both sides.
PR:L - nfnetlink requires CAP_NET_ADMIN in the target network namespace, and an unprivileged local user can reasonably obtain that via a user plus network namespace on affected deployments.
UI:N - No victim action is required after the attacker can send the netlink requests.
S:U - This is a kernel memory safety issue within the same host security authority and does not cross a VM, IOMMU, or similar scope boundary.
C:H - The bug is a use-after-free of the master struct nf_conn reachable from a retained expectation, and kernel UAFs can be leveraged for disclosure of sensitive kernel memory.
I:H - The stale master pointer is kernel heap memory corruption/use-after-free, which is defensibly exploitable for control-flow or data modification with heap grooming.
A:H - Even without full exploitation, dereferencing the freed master conntrack can trigger a kernel oops or panic.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

netfilter: ctnetlink: ensure safe access to master conntrack

Holding reference on the expectation is not sufficient, the master
conntrack object can just go away, making exp->master invalid.

To access exp->master safely:

- Grab the nf_conntrack_expect_lock, this gets serialized with
  clean_from_lists() which also holds this lock when the master
  conntrack goes away.

- Hold reference on master conntrack via nf_conntrack_find_get().
  Not so easy since the master tuple to look up for the master conntrack
  is not available in the existing problematic paths.

This patch goes for extending the nf_conntrack_expect_lock section
to address this issue for simplicity, in the cases that are described
below this is just slightly extending the lock section.

The add expectation command already holds a reference to the master
conntrack from ctnetlink_create_expect().

However, the delete expectation command needs to grab the spinlock
before looking up for the expectation. Expand the existing spinlock
section to address this to cover the expectation lookup. Note that,
the nf_ct_expect_iterate_net() calls already grabs the spinlock while
iterating over the expectation table, which is correct.

The get expectation command needs to grab the spinlock to ensure master
conntrack does not go away. This also expands the existing spinlock
section to cover the expectation lookup too. I needed to move the
netlink skb allocation out of the spinlock to keep it GFP_KERNEL.

For the expectation events, the IPEXP_DESTROY event is already delivered
under the spinlock, just move the delivery of IPEXP_NEW under the
spinlock too because the master conntrack event cache is reached through
exp->master.

While at it, add lockdep notations to help identify what codepaths need
to grab the spinlock.

descriptions.value: exiftool-vendored provides cross-platform Node.js access to ExifTool. Prior to 35.19.0, exiftool-vendored starts ExifTool in -stay_open True -@ - mode, where arguments are read from stdin one per line. In affected versions, several caller-supplied strings were interpolated into ExifTool arguments without rejecting line delimiters. A newline or carriage return inside one of those strings could split a single intended argument into multiple ExifTool arguments, allowing argument injection. The fix also rejects NUL bytes as unsafe control characters. Applications that pass attacker-controlled strings to affected APIs may allow an attacker to make ExifTool read files accessible to the ExifTool process, or write output to attacker-chosen file system paths accessible to that process. No remote code execution has been demonstrated. This vulnerability is fixed in 35.19.0.

cna.title: bpf: sockmap: Fix use-after-free of sk->sk_socket in sk_psock_verdict_data_ready().

scenarios.value:
AV:L - The vulnerable callback is reached through local BPF sockmap setup and local AF_UNIX send/close activity, not by unauthenticated network packets alone.
AC:L - The attacker can create the socketpair, install the sockmap verdict path, and race sendmsg against close/orphaning of the peer socket; both sides of the race are attacker-controlled.
PR:L - Creating and attaching the required sockmap/SK_SKB or SK_MSG BPF objects requires BPF/CAP_NET_ADMIN-style privileges, but these can be available to a low-privileged local user in delegated or user-namespace BPF deployments; choosing the higher severity option gives PR:L.
UI:N - No victim action is needed after the attacker has local execution and the required BPF access; triggering is done with attacker-controlled syscalls.
S:U - The impact is within the kernel security authority and represents ordinary kernel memory corruption or privilege escalation, not a cross-scope boundary such as guest-to-host escape.
C:H - This is a use-after-free of the socket object used to fetch proto_ops, and kernel UAFs can be shaped into information disclosure primitives.
I:H - The stale socket pointer can lead to use of attacker-influenced freed memory and function-pointer-oriented control flow, making arbitrary modification or code execution defensible.
A:H - The reported KASAN splat demonstrates a kernel use-after-free reachable from sendmsg, and repeated triggering can crash or destabilize the kernel.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

bpf: sockmap: Fix use-after-free of sk->sk_socket in sk_psock_verdict_data_ready().

syzbot reported use-after-free of AF_UNIX socket's sk->sk_socket
in sk_psock_verdict_data_ready(). [0]

In unix_stream_sendmsg(), the peer socket's ->sk_data_ready() is
called after dropping its unix_state_lock().

Although the sender socket holds the peer's refcount, it does not
prevent the peer's sock_orphan(), and the peer's sk_socket might
be freed after one RCU grace period.

Let's fetch the peer's sk->sk_socket and sk->sk_socket->ops under
RCU in sk_psock_verdict_data_ready().

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's netfilter component, specifically within the `nft_set_pipapo_avx2` AVX2 matching functions. This vulnerability occurs when a `pipapo` set with an 'ipv4 . port' key is reloaded. cna.title: netfilter: nft_set_pipapo_avx2: don't return non-matching entry on expiry

scenarios.value:
AV:N - Although nftables configuration is local, the vulnerable AVX2 pipapo lookup is also used from nftables packet hooks, so a received network packet can exercise it in a deployed firewall ruleset.
AC:L - No race, memory-layout dependency, or probabilistic condition is required once an affected AVX2 interval/concatenated set with expired or inactive entries exists; the attacker controls the packet key values used for lookup.
PR:N - A remote packet sender does not need nftables privileges or authentication to trigger the packet-path lookup in an already configured firewall.
UI:N - No victim user action is needed; packet processing and set lookup occur automatically in the kernel netfilter hook path.
S:U - The impact remains within the kernel/network filtering security authority and does not cross a VM, IOMMU, or separate sandbox boundary.
C:H - The bug can falsely match a non-matching set element after an expired or inactive element is skipped, which can bypass firewall policy and expose services or traffic that should have been unreachable.
I:H - A false nftables set match can select the wrong verdict or map data, allowing unauthorized traffic/action contrary to the intended firewall policy.
A:L - The same wrong-match behavior can cause legitimate nftables updates to fail with false element clashes or can misclassify selected traffic, but it is not a kernel crash, hang, or memory corruption.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

netfilter: nft_set_pipapo_avx2: don't return non-matching entry on expiry

New test case fails unexpectedly when avx2 matching functions are used.

The test first loads a ranomly generated pipapo set
with 'ipv4 . port' key, i.e.  nft -f foo.

This works.  Then, it reloads the set after a flush:
(echo flush set t s; cat foo) | nft -f -

This is expected to work, because its the same set after all and it was
already loaded once.

But with avx2, this fails: nft reports a clashing element.

The reported clash is of following form:

    We successfully re-inserted
      a . b
      c . d

Then we try to insert a . d

avx2 finds the already existing a . d, which (due to 'flush set') is marked
as invalid in the new generation.  It skips the element and moves to next.

Due to incorrect masking, the skip-step finds the next matching
element *only considering the first field*,

i.e. we return the already reinserted "a . b", even though the
last field is different and the entry should not have been matched.

No such error is reported for the generic c implementation (no avx2) or when
the last field has to use the 'nft_pipapo_avx2_lookup_slow' fallback.

Bisection points to
7711f4bb4b36 ("netfilter: nft_set_pipapo: fix range overlap detection")
but that fix merely uncovers this bug.

Before this commit, the wrong element is returned, but erronously
reported as a full, identical duplicate.

The root-cause is too early return in the avx2 match functions.
When we process the last field, we should continue to process data
until the entire input size has been consumed to make sure no stale
bits remain in the map.

cna.title: netfilter: x_tables: ensure names are nul-terminated

scenarios.value:
AV:L - The vulnerable x_tables match validation is reached by local rule creation paths such as iptables setsockopt table replacement or nft_compat netlink rule creation, not by received network packets.
AC:L - A local attacker can deterministically submit a crafted match blob with a non-NUL-terminated cgroup path or rateest name; no race or victim state is required.
PR:L - The path requires CAP_NET_ADMIN in the target network namespace, but netfilter administration is reachable by an unprivileged user through user and network namespaces on systems allowing unprivileged user namespaces.
UI:N - After obtaining the local namespace privileges, the attacker directly invokes the rule insertion path without any victim action.
S:U - The issue affects kernel netfilter processing within the same host kernel security authority and does not cross a VM, hypervisor, or separate security scope boundary.
C:H - The bug feeds attacker-controlled fixed-size fields lacking a NUL terminator into C-string consumers, and affected kernels can read past the intended match field into adjacent kernel memory until a NUL is found. Because this out-of-bounds read is not strictly bounded to only a few bytes across affected versions, confidentiality is scored High.
I:N - The investigated paths show an out-of-bounds read/string validation failure during rule validation, with no write primitive or control-flow modification identified.
A:H - The unterminated C-string scan can run beyond the allocated rule data and fault or oops the kernel, producing a local denial of service that can be triggered repeatedly.

cna.title: WWBN AVideo: Password Hash Leaked in MobileManager OAuth Redirect URL Enables Account Takeover

descriptions.value: WWBN AVideo is an open source video platform. In versions up to and including 29.0, plugin/MobileManager/oauth2.php completes an OAuth login by sending an HTTP 302 Location: oauth2Success.php?user=<email>&pass=<HASH> where <HASH> is the victim's stored password hash (md5(hash("whirlpool", sha1(password)))) read directly from the users table. AVideo's own login endpoint (objects/login.json.php) accepts an encodedPass=1 flag that bypasses hashing and performs a direct string comparison between the supplied value and the stored hash. Anyone who captures the redirect URL — via server logs, referrer leakage, or browser history — therefore obtains a credential equivalent to the plaintext password and can fully take over the account, including admin accounts. Commit 977cd6930a97571a26da4239e25c8096dd4ecbc1 contains an updated fix.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/amdgpu: Fix use-after-free race in VM acquire

Replace non-atomic vm->process_info assignment with cmpxchg()
to prevent race when parent/child processes sharing a drm_file
both try to acquire the same VM after fork().

(cherry picked from commit c7c573275ec20db05be769288a3e3bb2250ec618)

scenarios.value:
AV:L - The vulnerable path is reached through local AMD KFD/amdgpu device ioctls, especially acquiring an amdgpu render-node VM through /dev/kfd. No network or physical-device packet path reaches this code.
AC:L - The race is between attacker-controlled processes sharing the same drm_file after fork and issuing concurrent VM-acquire operations. Because the attacker controls both sides of the race, this is low complexity.
PR:L - An unprivileged local user with access to /dev/kfd and the amdgpu render node can issue the relevant ioctls; no real root or init-namespace capability check is required. This is basic local user access rather than administrative privilege.
UI:N - Exploitation does not require a victim user action after the attacker has local execution and device access. The attacker can open the device files, fork, and invoke the ioctls directly.
S:U - The bug corrupts kernel driver state within the same kernel security authority. It is a standard local kernel memory-corruption/privilege-escalation scenario, not a VM escape or other scope change.
C:H - The non-atomic VM ownership assignment can leave stale amdkfd_process_info references and cause a kernel use-after-free. Following kernel UAF scoring guidance, this can be leveraged for high-impact information disclosure.
I:H - The freed process_info object contains list, mutex, fence, and process state used later by KFD/GPUVM paths, making this kernel memory corruption. A defensible worst case is arbitrary kernel memory modification or control-flow influence.
A:H - Even without full exploitation, the UAF and associated list/lifetime corruption can crash or hang the kernel. Kernel oops/panic-level denial of service is high availability impact.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

crypto: pcrypt - Fix handling of MAY_BACKLOG requests

MAY_BACKLOG requests can return EBUSY.  Handle them by checking
for that value and filtering out EINPROGRESS notifications.

scenarios.value:
AV:N - pcrypt AEAD can sit under network-facing kernel crypto consumers such as kTLS/TIPC that process peer-supplied records or packets. In the highest reasonable deployment, a remote peer can drive the vulnerable encrypt/decrypt path through network traffic.
AC:L - The trigger is child crypto backlog behavior under `CRYPTO_TFM_REQ_MAY_BACKLOG`; an attacker can induce queue pressure with concurrent requests or traffic. There is no race that depends on conditions outside the attacker's control.
PR:N - The network-facing path requires no kernel privileges from the remote peer. The local AF_ALG AEAD path also has no capability gate, but the higher-severity network scenario is defensible.
UI:N - No victim interaction is required once the affected crypto consumer is configured. The attacker only sends data or submits crypto requests.
S:U - The bug corrupts kernel crypto/request state within the same kernel security authority. It is not a VM escape, IOMMU bypass, or other scope-changing boundary crossing.
C:H - Mishandling `-EBUSY` can complete and free the request while the child request remains queued, leading to use-after-free on later callbacks. A kernel UAF is reasonably exploitable for high-impact information disclosure.
I:H - The stale callback reuses freed request/padata memory and can drive list operations and completion paths on attacker-reclaimed objects. This is memory corruption with a plausible path to arbitrary write or control-flow corruption.
A:H - At minimum, the premature completion and later queued callback can dereference or manipulate freed kernel memory. That can produce kernel oops/panic or list corruption, giving high availability impact.

cna.title: wger: Privilege escalation via trainer-login session chaining allows gym trainers to impersonate gym managers

descriptions.value: wger is a free, open-source workout and fitness manager. In versions prior to 2.6, a gym trainer can escalate their session to any higher-privileged account (gym manager, general manager) by chaining two calls to the trainer-login endpoint. Once a trainer performs a legitimate switch into a low-privileged user, the session flag trainer.identity is set and this flag alone bypasses the permission check on all subsequent trainer-login calls. This grants full gym administration capabilities including viewing all member data, modifying contracts, managing gym configuration, and accessing other trainers' and managers' personal information. This issue has been fixed in version 2.6.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: nexthop: fix percpu use-after-free in remove_nh_grp_entry

When removing a nexthop from a group, remove_nh_grp_entry() publishes
the new group via rcu_assign_pointer() then immediately frees the
removed entry's percpu stats with free_percpu(). However, the
synchronize_net() grace period in the caller remove_nexthop_from_groups()
runs after the free. RCU readers that entered before the publish still
see the old group and can dereference the freed stats via
nh_grp_entry_stats_inc() -> get_cpu_ptr(nhge->stats), causing a
use-after-free on percpu memory.

Fix by deferring the free_percpu() until after synchronize_net() in the
caller. Removed entries are chained via nh_list onto a local deferred
free list. After the grace period completes and all RCU readers have
finished, the percpu stats are safely freed.

scenarios.value:
AV:L - The freeing side is reached through `RTM_DELNEXTHOP` over rtnetlink, which is a local netlink configuration interface. Remote packets can hit the RCU read side, but an attacker must locally trigger nexthop deletion to create the UAF.
AC:L - A local attacker can create nexthop groups, attach routes, generate concurrent route lookups, and delete a member nexthop, controlling both sides of the race. The bug is a straightforward RCU grace-period violation rather than a condition dependent on external state.
PR:L - The rtnetlink non-GET path requires `CAP_NET_ADMIN` in the socket's network namespace. Because this is reachable with namespaced `CAP_NET_ADMIN` via user/network namespaces on affected systems, this is Low rather than High.
UI:N - No victim interaction is required once the attacker has local access and the needed namespace capability. The attacker can perform the netlink operations and traffic generation directly.
S:U - The vulnerability corrupts kernel memory within the same kernel security authority. It is a kernel privilege-impact bug, not a VM escape or cross-scope boundary bypass.
C:H - This is a use-after-free of per-CPU nexthop group statistics reachable from RCU route readers. Following kernel CVSS guidance, UAF memory corruption is treated as enabling high confidentiality impact.
I:H - The stale reader writes packet counters and sequence state through a freed per-CPU pointer, creating memory corruption that can plausibly be shaped into write/control-flow impact. Per the required guidance, UAF is scored as High integrity impact.
A:H - The stale dereference of freed per-CPU memory can crash or otherwise destabilize the kernel. Any kernel UAF with crash potential is High availability impact.

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

usb: class: cdc-wdm: fix reordering issue in read code path

Quoting the bug report:

Due to compiler optimization or CPU out-of-order execution, the
desc->length update can be reordered before the memmove. If this
happens, wdm_read() can see the new length and call copy_to_user() on
uninitialized memory. This also violates LKMM data race rules [1].

Fix it by using WRITE_ONCE and memory barriers.

An integer overflow was addressed with improved input validation. This issue is fixed in macOS Golden Gate 27. Processing a maliciously crafted file may lead to a denial-of-service or potentially disclose memory contents.

cna.title: Revert "PCI/IOV: Add PCI rescan-remove locking when enabling/disabling SR-IOV"

descriptions.value:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Revert "PCI/IOV: Add PCI rescan-remove locking when enabling/disabling SR-IOV"

This reverts commit 05703271c3cd ("PCI/IOV: Add PCI rescan-remove locking
when enabling/disabling SR-IOV"), which causes a deadlock by recursively
taking pci_rescan_remove_lock when sriov_del_vfs() is called as part of
pci_stop_and_remove_bus_device(). For example with the following sequence
of commands:

  $ echo <NUM> > /sys/bus/pci/devices/<pf>/sriov_numvfs
  $ echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/<pf>/remove

A trimmed trace of the deadlock on a mlx5 device is as below:

  zsh/5715 is trying to acquire lock:
  000002597926ef50 (pci_rescan_remove_lock){+.+.}-{3:3}, at: sriov_disable+0x34/0x140

  but task is already holding lock:
  000002597926ef50 (pci_rescan_remove_lock){+.+.}-{3:3}, at: pci_stop_and_remove_bus_device_locked+0x24/0x80
  ...
  Call Trace:
   [<00000259778c4f90>] dump_stack_lvl+0xc0/0x110
   [<00000259779c844e>] print_deadlock_bug+0x31e/0x330
   [<00000259779c1908>] __lock_acquire+0x16c8/0x32f0
   [<00000259779bffac>] lock_acquire+0x14c/0x350
   [<00000259789643a6>] __mutex_lock_common+0xe6/0x1520
   [<000002597896413c>] mutex_lock_nested+0x3c/0x50
   [<00000259784a07e4>] sriov_disable+0x34/0x140
   [<00000258f7d6dd80>] mlx5_sriov_disable+0x50/0x80 [mlx5_core]
   [<00000258f7d5745e>] remove_one+0x5e/0xf0 [mlx5_core]
   [<00000259784857fc>] pci_device_remove+0x3c/0xa0
   [<000002597851012e>] device_release_driver_internal+0x18e/0x280
   [<000002597847ae22>] pci_stop_bus_device+0x82/0xa0
   [<000002597847afce>] pci_stop_and_remove_bus_device_locked+0x5e/0x80
   [<00000259784972c2>] remove_store+0x72/0x90
   [<0000025977e6661a>] kernfs_fop_write_iter+0x15a/0x200
   [<0000025977d7241c>] vfs_write+0x24c/0x300
   [<0000025977d72696>] ksys_write+0x86/0x110
   [<000002597895b61c>] __do_syscall+0x14c/0x400
   [<000002597896e0ee>] system_call+0x6e/0x90

This alone is not a complete fix as it restores the issue the cited commit
tried to solve. A new fix will be provided as a follow on.

cna.title: Rsync < 3.4.3 Symlink Race Condition via Path-Based Syscalls

descriptions.value: Rsync version 3.4.2 and prior contain symlink race condition vulnerabilities in path-based system calls including chmod, lchown, utimes, rename, unlink, mkdir, symlink, mknod, link, rmdir, and lstat that allow local attackers to redirect operations to files outside the exported rsync module. Attackers with local filesystem access can exploit the timing window between path resolution and syscall execution by swapping symlinks to apply sender-supplied permissions, ownership, timestamps, or filenames to arbitrary files outside the intended module boundary on rsync daemons configured with 'use chroot = no'.

cna.title: Starman versions before 0.4019 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via quadratic regex backtracking when parsing chunked request bodies

solutions.value: Upgrade to Starman 0.4019 or later.

descriptions.value:
Starman versions before 0.4019 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via quadratic regex backtracking when parsing chunked request bodies.

Starman decodes chunked request bodies before calling the application, matching each chunk-size line with `s/^(([0-9a-fA-F]+).*\015\012)//`. A line of hex digits followed by a bare LF and then CRLF never matches, because `.` does not match LF, and each failed attempt backtracks in time quadratic in the length of the hex run. Nothing limits the length of the line.

A remote attacker can exhaust worker CPU by sending such requests to any route.

cna.title: Use of Cache Containing Sensitive Information in Elasticsearch Leading to Information Disclosure

descriptions.value: Use of Cache Containing Sensitive Information (CWE-524) in Elasticsearch can lead to information disclosure and incorrect search results via specially crafted search requests. For some query types, Elasticsearch can share cached query results between users who have field-level security restrictions and users who do not. A user restricted by field-level security can learn which documents match a value in a field that they cannot read. A restricted user can also cause users with full access to receive incomplete search results. Disclosure is only possible when a user with full access ran the same query on the same shard recently.

cna.title: vLLM: DoS via unbounded chat_template Jinja2 rendering exhausts the renderer thread pool

descriptions.value: vLLM is an inference and serving engine for large language models. From 0.19.0 until 0.32.0, authenticated callers can supply a request chat template when no server-side --chat-template is configured, or a malicious model repository can provide a template that is compiled and rendered by tokenizer.apply_chat_template() without a wall-clock timeout, output-size limit, or iteration bound. Rendering runs in a ThreadPoolExecutor with one worker by default, so a nonterminating render can block /v1/responses and other chat-template users after the request ends, while an output-expanding render can exhaust server memory. Harmony models are not affected because they do not use this Jinja path. This issue is fixed in version 0.32.0.

cna.title: baserCMS: BcCustomContent file fields can be configured to allow executable file extensions such as php, leading to arbitrary PHP file upload

descriptions.value: baserCMS is a website development framework. Starting in version 5.0.0-beta1 and prior to versions 5.3.2 and 5.4.2, `PermissionGroupsService::build()` reads a plugin's `config/permission.php` to decide what each user group may reach. When that file is absent it writes a wildcard allow rule instead: `url` `/baser/<prefix>/<plugin>/*`, `method` `*`, `auth` true, for every non-admin group. BcCustomContent has no such file in any release. After an administrator installs it, the default `operators` group can store and execute arbitrary PHP under the document root. Versions 5.3.2 and 5.4.2 patch the issue.

descriptions.description: CWE-434: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type

cna.title: LangGraph CLI prints the registry push token in `langgraph deploy --verbose` output

descriptions.value: The LangGraph CLI is the official command-line interface for LangGraph. From 0.4.15 until 0.4.32, langgraph deploy --verbose passes a temporary registry push token on standard input to docker login --password-stdin, but the CLI subprocess helper prints command input in verbose mode. Anyone who can read resulting CI logs or terminal recordings before the token's maximum 12-hour expiration can pull deployment images or push images to that deployment's image repository. Deployments without --verbose and remote image builds are not affected, and the token alone cannot update a deployment to execute a pushed image. This issue is fixed in version 0.4.32.

cna.title: Zimbra Collaboration Suite Shared-File Mailbox Quota Accounting Error Enables Quota Exhaustion

credits.value: Jonah Burgess (CryptoCat), Senior Security Researcher, Rapid7

descriptions.value: A mailbox quota-accounting vulnerability in Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) allows an authenticated user to consume another user’s mailbox quota by repeatedly sharing and revoking a document. Creation of the recipient’s shared-file record charges the document size to mailbox-wide usage. Revocation deletes the record and reverses its folder counters without reversing the mailbox-wide charge. Repeated normal share notifications therefore accumulate quota usage after the visible records are gone. On accounts with a finite quota, this can prevent incoming mail and other size-increasing operations without recipient interaction. The issue affects ZCS 10.1.16 and 10.1.20.

cna.title: Starlet versions from 0.20 before 0.33 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via regular expression backtracking when decoding chunked request bodies

solutions.value: Upgrade to Starlet 0.33 or later.

descriptions.value:
Starlet versions from 0.20 before 0.33 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via regular expression backtracking when decoding chunked request bodies.

A chunk-size line is matched as a run of hex digits, then .* and a CRLF. A run followed by a bare LF and then a CRLF can never match, and the engine retries the match once for each digit, so the time taken grows with the square of the run length. Nothing limits the length of the run, which can span several reads.

A remote attacker can occupy a worker for about a minute of CPU time with one 128 KiB request, before the application is called.

descriptions.value:
Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in the HTTP/2 request body reader of mtrudel bandit allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to hold stream processes open indefinitely via WINDOW_UPDATE or empty SETTINGS frames sent while a Plug reads the request body.

Bandit.HTTP2.Stream.do_read_data/4 in lib/bandit/http2/stream.ex waits for each frame with a fresh read_timeout. A stream WINDOW_UPDATE, or the zero-delta window update that every empty SETTINGS frame delivers to all streams, ends the wait without delivering any body data, and the loop starts a new full countdown. A client that sends one of these 9-byte frames before each countdown expires keeps read_body blocked, together with the stream process and whatever the application holds while reading, for as long as it likes.

This issue affects bandit: from 1.4.0 before 1.14.0.

1. Run Bandit with a Plug that calls `Plug.Conn.read_body/2`.
2. Open an HTTP/2 connection and send HEADERS for `POST /` on stream 1 without END_STREAM.
3. Every 10 seconds, send a WINDOW_UPDATE on stream 1 with an increment of 1.
4. The stream stays open for 120 s, eight times the default 15 s `read_timeout`. Without the WINDOW_UPDATE frames, the server ends the read after about 15 s.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Per-receive timeout. Bandit.HTTP2.Stream.read_data/2 passes a flat read_timeout (default 15,000 ms) to do_read_data/4, which blocks in do_recv/2's receive ... after timeout.

2. Non-progress frames end the wait. A stream WINDOW_UPDATE, delivered through Bandit.HTTP2.Connection.handle_frame/3, or an empty SETTINGS frame, which delivers a zero-delta window update to every stream, is matched inside that receive. do_recv_send_window_update/2 returns a bare %Stream{}, and do_read_data/4 recurses with the identical timeout, restarting the countdown.

3. Nothing else bounds the read. The transport read timeout fires only when no bytes arrive, max_bytes is decremented only by DATA frames, and neither WINDOW_UPDATE nor SETTINGS frames are rate limited. The send path in do_send_data/4 uses a progress-based deadline; the read path does not.

cna.title: Starman versions before 0.4019 for Perl send response bodies for HEAD requests, desynchronizing responses on keep-alive connections

solutions.value: Upgrade to Starman 0.4019 or later.

workarounds.value: For deployments that cannot upgrade to 0.4019, enable Plack::Middleware::Head, which removes the body from HEAD responses.

descriptions.value:
Starman versions before 0.4019 for Perl send response bodies for HEAD requests, desynchronizing responses on keep-alive connections.

For a HEAD request Starman omits chunked framing but still writes the body returned by the application, on both the array and streaming response paths. Responses with a 1xx, 204 or 304 status also carry the body.

On a keep-alive or pipelined connection the client reads those bytes as the start of the next response. A front-end proxy that reuses upstream connections may then pair responses with the wrong requests.

cna.title: Out-of-bounds read of DCP block header in DCP Set and Identify request parsing

solutions.value: Upgrade to P-Net 1.0.3 or later.

supportingMedia.value: Upgrade to P-Net 1.0.3 or later.

descriptions.value: P-Net before 1.0.3 does not check that a complete block header is present in the received data before reading the next block in DCP Set and Identify requests. In addition, a DCP Set block with a length smaller than the two-byte block qualifier makes the length underflow, so the block is processed with a length of 65534 bytes. This can cause a crash (denial of service) or disclose a small amount of memory content. Requires ADJACENT network access.

descriptions.value: Backstage is an open framework for building developer portals. cna.title: Tornado: Event loop blocking and excess memory use from chunked bodies with many small chunks

descriptions.value: Tornado is a Python web framework and asynchronous networking library. Prior to 6.6.0, Tornado decodes HTTP/1.1 chunked transfer encoding by processing body data that has already arrived without yielding to the event loop. A remote unauthenticated peer can send millions of one-byte chunks to monopolize the process event loop and stall every other connection served by that process, while lowering max_body_size only limits the duration of each request. For handlers that do not use @stream_request_body, retaining each chunk as a separate object can consume roughly twenty times the received body size, and SimpleAsyncHTTPClient has the same event-loop behavior when reading a response from a malicious server. This issue is fixed in version 6.6.0.

cna.title: Apache ZooKeeper: Unbounded recursion in snapshot serialization allows a client to render the server unrecoverable

credits.value: Sai Sreewathsa Kovalluri, Shon Babu, and Kannan K of Innspark Solutions (https://innspark.in/)
Prasath Jayasundar & PayPal Cyber Security Team

descriptions.value:
Uncontrolled recursion in Apache ZooKeeper. The server serializes its data tree to a snapshot by recursing one stack frame per znode level, with no depth bound. A client permitted to create znodes (the default root ACL is open) can build a chain of nested znodes deep enough that taking a snapshot exhausts the JVM stack and kills the snapshot thread; sizes stay within jute.maxbuffer, so existing limits do not prevent it. This is a denial of service that becomes persistent: on restart the server rebuilds the deep tree from its transaction log and fails again while taking the startup snapshot, so it does not return to service, and recovery can entail data loss. The same log affects a leader and its followers, so it can spread across an ensemble.

This issue affects Apache ZooKeeper 3.8.0 through 3.8.7 and 3.9.0 through 3.9.6. Users are recommended to upgrade to 3.8.8 or 3.9.7, which fix the issue. As a workaround, use ACLs and authentication to restrict znode creation rather than relying on the default open root ACL.

cna.title: epiphany: TLS certificate warning bypass via race in tlsErrorPage message handler

credits.value: Red Hat would like to thank Fernando Munoz for reporting this issue.

workarounds.value: Until a fixed Epiphany build is installed, avoid following links from untrusted sites to HTTPS destinations, and do not rely on Epiphany for sensitive sites when browsing untrusted content. Restrict network access for untrusted browsing where practical (https://cmetaxonomy.org/entries/CME-203.html). Restarting the browser clears any attacker-installed certificate exceptions for the session.

descriptions.value:
A race condition in Epiphany allows a malicious website to bypass the TLS/SSL certificate warning page.

Epiphany registers the main-world script message handler "tlsErrorPage" so its internal TLS error page can implement "Accept Risk and Proceed". The handler was registered immediately before loading the error page, leaving a brief window where the previously loaded untrusted origin could still call window.webkit.messageHandlers.tlsErrorPage.postMessage(...). The only authorization check compares a numeric WebKit page id that increments predictably; an attacker can burst-guess ids and approve a certificate exception with no user click.

If a victim visits malicious site A that redirects to site B with an invalid certificate, site A can, for a few milliseconds, disable TLS certificate error warnings for host B until Epiphany is restarted, enabling man-in-the-middle or site spoofing for that host.

Upstream report: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/epiphany/-/work_items/2978
Proof of concept: https://beford.net/poc/ssl_poc.html
Fix: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/epiphany/-/merge_requests/2245 (register handlers on LOAD_COMMITTED). No fixed release tagged yet; reporter and maintainer describe all current versions as affected. Maintainer notes the risky registration timing dates to commit 1da1caed (Epiphany 45.x era); before that the handlers were always registered and similarly reachable from web content.

cna.title: zip: legacy Shrink/Reduce/Implode decoder: denial of service from attacker-controlled ZIP64 uncompressed size

descriptions.value: zip is a zip library for Rust that supports reading and writing simple ZIP files. From 5.1.0 until 9.0.0, applications built with the legacy-zip feature can reserve output capacity from an attacker-controlled ZIP64 uncompressed size before validating the compressed stream. The ShrinkDecoder path in src/legacy/shrink.rs can panic with a capacity overflow during ZipArchive::extract, and the Reduce and Implode decoders contain the same unbounded preallocation pattern. An unhandled panic can terminate an archive-processing service. This issue is fixed in version 9.0.0.

cna.title: zip: Unbounded Symlink-Target Handling Can Abort Or Exhaust Memory During Extraction

descriptions.value: zip is a zip library for Rust that supports reading and writing simple ZIP files. From 1.3.0 until 9.0.0, ZipArchive::extract in src/read/mod.rs calls Vec::with_capacity for a symbolic link target using the attacker-controlled ZIP64 uncompressed_size before reading entry data. A small archive can request an impossible capacity, causing the infallible allocation path to abort the process before the entry is validated. The failure cannot be contained with catch_unwind or a worker thread, allowing repeated denial of service in archive-processing applications. This issue is fixed in version 9.0.0.

workarounds.value:
Decode untrusted JSON with an integer decoder that rejects long digit runs before conversion:

defmodule SafeJSON do
  def decode!(binary) do
    case JSON.decode(binary, :ok, integer: &safe_integer/1) do
      {decoded, :ok, ""} -> decoded
      _ -> raise ArgumentError, "invalid JSON"
    end
  end

  defp safe_integer(digits) when byte_size(digits) <= 1024, do: String.to_integer(digits)
  defp safe_integer(_digits), do: raise(ArgumentError, "integer too long")
end

In Phoenix, pass SafeJSON to Plug.Parsers as json_decoder instead of Phoenix.json_library().

descriptions.value:
Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input vulnerability in the Elixir standard library's JSON module allows an unauthenticated attacker who supplies a JSON document to cause a denial of service through CPU and memory exhaustion.

JSON.decode/1 and JSON.decode!/1 convert each integer literal with erlang:binary_to_integer/1 and do not bound its length. A literal of one million digits decodes successfully but costs 100 to 300 times as much CPU as a string of the same length, so one request body of a few megabytes holds a scheduler for about a second. A literal of more than about 1.29 million digits raises SystemLimitError. Applications generated by phx.new decode request bodies with JSON in Plug.Parsers, before routing and authentication.

This issue affects elixir: from 1.18.0-rc.0 before 1.18.6, from 1.19.0-rc.0 before 1.19.7, and from 1.20.0-rc.0 before 1.20.5.

x_technicalAnalysis.value:
1. Default integer decoder

JSON.decode/1 and JSON.decode!/1 call JSON.decode/3 without an integer decoder. Up to the removal of Erlang/OTP 26 support, JSON.decode/3 used the vendored elixir_json module, whose default is fun erlang:binary_to_integer/1. It now calls OTP's :json.decode/3, which has the same default. The JSON.decode/3 documentation names &String.to_integer/1 as the default, which converts the same way.

2. Unbounded conversion

The decoder scans the digits of an integer literal and passes the whole run to the conversion. Nothing limits the run's length, so the cost grows faster than linearly with the number of digits. At one million digits an integer literal costs 100 to 300 times as much CPU as a string literal of the same length. Above about 1.29 million digits the conversion raises SystemLimitError, which JSON.decode/3 does not catch.

3. Reach

phx.new sets config :phoenix, :json_library, JSON, and the generated endpoint passes Phoenix.json_library() to Plug.Parsers as json_decoder. Plug.Parsers runs before routing and authentication and accepts bodies up to 8 MB by default. It rescues the SystemLimitError into a 400 response after the CPU cost is spent. Jason, the previous default, rejects integer literals longer than its decoding_integer_digit_limit (1024 by default) before conversion.

At one million digits an integer literal costs 100 to 300 times as much CPU as a string literal of the same length. Above about 1.29 million digits the conversion raises SystemLimitError, which JSON.decode/3 does not catch.

3. Reach

phx.new sets config :phoenix, :json_library, JSON, and the generated endpoint passes Phoenix.json_library() to Plug.Parsers as json_decoder. Plug.Parsers runs before routing and authentication and accepts bodies up to 8 MB by default. It rescues the SystemLimitError into a 400 response after the CPU cost is spent. Jason, the previous default, rejects integer literals longer than its decoding_integer_digit_limit (1024 by default) before conversion.

**1. Default integer decoder**

`JSON.decode/1` and `JSON.decode!/1` call `JSON.decode/3` without an `integer` decoder. Up to the removal of Erlang/OTP 26 support, `JSON.decode/3` used the vendored `elixir_json` module, whose default is `fun erlang:binary_to_integer/1`. It now calls OTP's `:json.decode/3`, which has the same default. The `JSON.decode/3` documentation names `&String.to_integer/1` as the default, which converts the same way.

descriptions.value: The Prime Mover – Backup and Migration plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to PHP Object Injection in all versions up to, and including, 2.2.1 via deserialization of untrusted input in the migration search-and-replace routine (recursiveUnserializeReplace()). An unauthenticated attacker can store a crafted, base64-encoded serialized object in wp_comments.comment_content through the standard comment-submission endpoint (wp-comments-post.php). When an administrator subsequently performs a routine Prime Mover export or restore, the plugin base64-decodes that stored value and passes it to unserialize() with no allowed_classes restriction. A Property-Oriented Programming (POP) chain is present in the plugin's own bundled Freemius library (FS_Clone_Manager::__set → FS_Option_Manager::set_option → store() → update_option()), so no additional plugin or theme is required — the plugin ships the gadget itself.

cna.title: Serialize JavaScript: Cross-site scripting (XSS) via unescaped </script at the end of a serialized function body

descriptions.value: Serialize JavaScript serializes JavaScript values to a superset of JSON that includes regular expressions and functions. Prior to 7.1.3, the function-source escaping logic does not neutralize a bare closing-script prefix when attacker-influenced function source text ends exactly at that prefix. Because each function body is escaped independently, a delimiter supplied by surrounding serialized output can terminate an HTML script element, and a later serialized value supplies injected markup that becomes a live element in the page. Exploitation requires control of a serialized function's source text, such as through a spoofed toString(). This issue is fixed in version 7.1.3.

descriptions.value: A flaw was found in the iscsiuio component of open-iscsi. descriptions.value: Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) is an open standard for machine learning interoperability. From 1.4.0 until 1.22.0, ScanInferenceFunction, ScanInferenceFunction_opset8, and ScanInferenceFunction_opset9 do not safely validate the required num_scan_inputs attribute. cna.title: XS::libbrotli versions before 1.2.1.0 for Perl bundle a brotli library with an out-of-bounds write in the decoder

solutions.value: Upgrade to XS-libbrotli 1.2.1.0 or later and reinstall every XS module built against it.

descriptions.value:
XS::libbrotli versions before 1.2.1.0 for Perl bundle a brotli library with an out-of-bounds write in the decoder.

Affected versions compile a bundled brotli into static archives that dependent XS modules link against at build time, rather than using the system library. The bundled copy, 1.0.7 or 1.1.0 across the range, carries the decoder out-of-bounds write described in CVE-2026-111497. Version 1.2.1.0 updates it to brotli 1.2.1.

XS::libbrotli has no Perl interface, so the decoder is reached through any dependent module that decompresses untrusted data with it. An attacker supplying a crafted brotli stream can corrupt decoder state, disclose memory, crash the process, or potentially execute arbitrary code. Upgrading the system brotli does not remediate this.

cna.title: Rembg: Unauthenticated SAM model injection permits local-file disclosure through malicious ONNX graphs

descriptions.value: Rembg is a tool to remove images background. Prior to 2.0.82, the public /api/remove endpoint passes attacker-controlled extras.sam_model through rembg/commands/s_command.py to rembg/sessions/sam.py, where it is interpolated into SAM filenames and GitHub download URLs passed to pooch.retrieve() without a pinned hash. An unauthenticated attacker can supply a sam_model value combining path traversal with URL fragment syntax to exploit the HTTP request discarding the fragment while the local POSIX path retains it. The first request primes the attacker-selected path tree, and an identical repeated request downloads malicious ONNX encoder and decoder files beside a readable target file. The graphs can load the target through ONNX external data and encode its bytes into the returned PNG mask, disclosing complete files accessible to the rembg process and allowing arbitrary ONNX computation. This issue is fixed in version 2.0.82.

descriptions.description: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

descriptions.value: baserCMS is a website development framework. In versions 5.0.0 before 5.3.2 and 5.4.0 before 5.4.2, global shortcode expansion runs over the complete rendered page, including HTML-escaped blog comments supplied by unauthenticated visitors. A comment containing the BcBaser.getGoogleMaps shortcode can set apiBaseUrl to an attacker-controlled script URL, which is emitted as a script src and executes JavaScript on the site's origin when another visitor or administrator opens the article displaying that comment. Escaping raw HTML in comments does not prevent this stored cross-site scripting because shortcode processing happens after HTML rendering. Other registered shortcodes also expand in comments; Mail.getForm can embed a working contact form with a valid CSRF token. The flaw can compromise the authenticated browser context of an administrator who views the affected article. This issue has been patched in versions 5.3.2 and 5.4.2.

solutions.value: Upgrade to Starman 0.4019 or later.

descriptions.value:
Starman versions before 0.4019 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded buffering of chunked request bodies.

The chunked body decoder keeps each chunk in memory until the whole chunk and its CRLF have arrived, and sets no limit on the length of a chunk-size line. A client that declares a huge chunk size and streams data, or sends a chunk-size line that never ends, grows the buffer for as long as it keeps sending.

A remote attacker can exhaust worker memory with a single connection.

solutions.value: Upgrade to Starlet 0.33 or later.

descriptions.value:
Starlet versions before 0.33 for Perl allow a request declaring a large Content-Length to kill a worker by exhausting memory.

The request body is read in a loop that asks sysread for all of the remaining declared length at once. Perl grows the read buffer to that size before any data arrives, so a length larger than available memory makes the worker exit with an uncatchable out of memory error before the application is called.

A remote attacker can force a worker restart with each request of a few bytes.

cna.title: Arbitrary file read and backend crash through unrestricted provider method calls

descriptions.value: Any registered user can read any file the backend process can read, with the result returned as bytes so binary files work.

The backend's environment is readable, which exposes the JWT signing secret, the database and Redis connection strings and the credentials and API keys of connected providers when they are passed as environment variables.

With the JWT signing secret an attacker can sign a session for any user, including a user in another organization or an instance super administrator, and can decrypt data the application stores encrypted with the same secret.
A single request ends the backend process, and it can be repeated after every restart.
Other provider functions become callable by any member of an organization that owns a channel, some of which return access tokens for the connected account that other routes keep server side.

exploits.value: Exploitation was demonstrated end to end against an unmodified build of Postiz at commit 3a7d28b7ad96, using only a self-registered account: the contents of a file placed outside the application's directories and the exact JWT secret the backend was started with were both returned in full. Terminating the backend with one request was demonstrated separately.

timeline.value: Anthropic has disclosed a thorough report of this vulnerability including a working PoC to Postiz
Postiz has reproduced the vulnerability and is working on a fix
Postiz has pushed a fix for this vulnerability and verified it
Postiz has created a release and published the advisory

workarounds.value: Set DISABLE_REGISTRATION=true. The attacker needs an ordinary account, so closing self-registration limits exposure to people who already hold one. This reduces reach, it does not close the issue.

descriptions.value:
Postiz lets a signed-in user ask the backend to run a function on one of their connected channels. The backend did not restrict which functions can be requested, so a user could call internal helper functions that were never meant to be reachable from the web interface.

One of those helpers reads a file from the server's disk. A user who connects a channel whose stored token is a file path can have the backend return the contents of any file it can read, including its environment, which holds the secret used to sign login sessions, the database address and the credentials of connected services. Another helper makes the backend process exit with a single request. Self-registration is open by default, so no existing account and no action by another user is needed.

configurations.value: The default configuration is affected and no setting has to be changed. Self-registration is open unless DISABLE_REGISTRATION is set to true; with registration closed, any existing user can still exploit the issue.
The image built from the project's Dockerfile.dev runs the process as root, so every file root can read is exposed. The process's own environment is readable regardless of the user it runs as.

descriptions.value: A path traversal vulnerability exists in the Mautic Asset API. When creating a local asset through the API, the supplied file path is not restricted to the asset upload directory. An authenticated API user with permission to create assets can register any file that is readable by the web server process as a Mautic asset. When the asset is published, its public download URL serves the contents of that file without authentication. This allows the attacker to read arbitrary files from the server, including Mautic configuration files containing the database password, secret key, and mail (SMTP) credentials, as well as system files and any other file readable by the web server user. Exposed credentials can be used to access the database or other connected services, and anyone with the public asset URL can retrieve the file contents.

descriptions.value: Mongoose is an embedded web server and network library. Prior to 7.22, mg_path_is_sane in src/util.c read path.buf[1] without first requiring path.len to be at least two and read s[2] when only two bytes remained. Unauthenticated remote requests reaching mg_http_upload or mg_http_serve_dir with the affected short path shapes could therefore trigger one-byte heap out-of-bounds reads. On bare-metal or RTOS targets without memory protection, the adjacent byte could be exposed or influence whether a path was accepted, and instrumented builds could crash. solutions.value: Upgrade to Starman 0.4019 or later.

descriptions.value:
Starman versions before 0.4019 for Perl allow a stalled request body to hold a worker indefinitely, as read_timeout covers only the headers.

Content-Length and chunked request bodies are read with blocking reads and no deadline. A client that sends complete headers and then stalls or trickles the body keeps the worker waiting until it disconnects.

A remote attacker can take every worker with a few such connections, five with the default worker count, so the server stops answering requests.

Version 0.4019 applies read_timeout to each wait for body data and adds a body_timeout limit, 300 seconds by default, on the total time to read a body.

cna.title: Python Social Auth: OpenID Connect nonce is not bound to the browser session, so a stolen authorization code logs the attacker in as the victim

descriptions.value: Python Social Auth is a social authentication and registration mechanism. Prior to 6.2.0, OpenIdConnectAuth in social_core/backends/open_id_connect.py uses get_and_store_nonce to place the OpenID Connect nonce in a shared OpenIdConnectAssociation table, and get_nonce and validate_claims verify only that the nonce exists and has not expired rather than binding it to the browser session and OAuth state that initiated the login. An attacker who obtains a victim's unused authorization code can start a separate login to obtain valid state for the attacker's browser, submit the victim's code with that state, and pass nonce validation because the victim nonce is globally available. With DEFAULT_USE_PKCE disabled in the default OpenIdConnectAuth configuration, the attacker can be logged in as the victim. This issue is fixed in version 6.2.0.

descriptions.description: CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity

descriptions.value: ConnMan through 2.0 has a stack-based buffer overflow via a DHCPv6 Reply message. This occurs in get_domains in gdhcp/client.c. It copies a fixed NS_MAXDNAME (1025) bytes from a DHCPv6 DOMAIN_LIST (option 24) value into a 1026-byte stack buffer dns_name regardless of the actual option length, then walks DNS labels with an unbounded "c += jump + 1" loop. A crafted DHCPv6 REPLY with a DOMAIN_LIST option of >= 1025 non-zero bytes makes the label walk leave the buffer and read/write '.' past its end in attacker-chosen strides. An on-link attacker can trigger this without authentication via a forged Router Advertisement (O=1) and a forged DHCPv6 REPLY matching xid/CLIENTID with a long DOMAIN_LIST. The impact is unauthenticated on-link crash of connmand (runs as root). This was introduced in bb06c47.

references.name: VDB-425983 | Kakao khaiii JSON Config File Linear.cpp open out-of-bounds
Submit #1022283 | Kakao khaiii commit 3d0c8944374163b1107fd6690ccf3a408430a02d (master, 2025-05-22; version 0.4) Out-of-bounds Read

descriptions.value: A security flaw has been discovered in Kakao khaiii up to 0.4. The impacted element is the function khaiii::nn::Linear::open of the file src/main/cpp/khaiii/nn/Linear.cpp of the component JSON Config File Handler. The manipulation of the argument hidden_dim/class_num results in out-of-bounds read. The attack requires a local approach. The exploit has been released to the public and may be used for attacks. The vendor explains: "khaiii treats the resource directory (--rsc-dir) as trusted input, like a binary or a shared library. To use this defect, an attacker must already be able to write to that directory. With that access, an attacker can change the analysis results without this defect." This vulnerability only affects products that are no longer supported by the maintainer.

descriptions.value: The Recipe Card Blocks Lite WordPress plugin before 3.6.4 does not perform an authorization check before rendering posts through its recipe print feature, allowing unauthenticated users to disclose the title, ID and recipe content of unpublished posts, including drafts, pending, private and password-protected posts, that contain a recipe card block. cna.title: ML-KEM key-pair lookup can bind an unrelated or attacker-planted public key, exposing encapsulated shared secrets

descriptions.value: In `github.com/eclipse-keypont/crypto11/v2` versions `>= 2.0.0-rc3, <= 2.0.0-rc8`, the ML-KEM key-pair lookup functions (`FindMLKEMKeyPair`, `FindMLKEMKeyPairs`, `FindMLKEMKeyPairsWithAttributes`) locate the public half of an ML-KEM key pair by `CKA_ID`/`CKA_LABEL` and never verify it against the private key. In addition, the "ID only" fallback search runs even when the private key has no `CKA_ID`, so the search template reduces to the public-key class and the ML-KEM key type and the first ML-KEM public key on the token is returned. `Encapsulate()` on the resulting key pair encrypts the fresh shared secret to that key, so its owner — not the holder of the private key the caller looked up — can recover the secret. An attacker who can open an unauthenticated session on the token and plant a public `CKK_ML_KEM` object carrying the victim's `CKA_ID`/`CKA_LABEL` receives the shared secrets for encapsulations performed through the substituted key pair, compromising the confidentiality of those secrets and of everything protected by keys derived from them. The v1 module paths have no ML-KEM support and are not affected.

descriptions.value: virtualenv is a tool for creating isolated virtual python environments. cna.title: HTTP::Server::PSGI versions before 1.0056 for Perl allow a single request to crash the server by declaring a large Content-Length

solutions.value: Upgrade to Plack 1.0057 or later.

descriptions.value:
HTTP::Server::PSGI versions before 1.0056 for Perl allow a single request to crash the server by declaring a large Content-Length.

The request body is read with sysread() calls sized by the remaining Content-Length. Perl grows the read buffer to the requested length before any data arrives, so the server tries to allocate as much memory as the client declares.

A remote attacker can send one request with a large Content-Length and a few body bytes, and perl exits with an out-of-memory error before the application is called. HTTP::Server::PSGI runs as a single process, so the server stays down until restarted.

cna.title: OpenEMR: Broken Access Control in controller.php Enables Insurance Routing Credential Hijack and PHI Enumeration

descriptions.value: OpenEMR is a free and open source electronic health records and medical practice management application. Prior to 8.3.0, library/classes/Controller.class.php allows explicit controller.php dispatch to controllers missing from CONTROLLER_ACL_MAP, and checkControllerAcl() returns without enforcing any permission for those entries. A low-privilege authenticated user can invoke C_X12Partner::edit_action_process() to create or alter insurance-routing hosts and credentials, or invoke C_PatientFinder::find_action_process() to enumerate patient names, dates of birth, and identifiers. The shared fail-open dispatcher root cause also exposes other administrative controllers that were intended to be reached through ACL-gated Practice Settings routes. This issue is fixed in version 8.3.0.

cna.title: Improper Certificate Validation in Elastic Docker Images Leading to Interception of TLS Connections

descriptions.value: CAPEC-474 Signature Spoofing by Key Theft

Improper Certificate Validation (CWE-295) in the operating system certificate bundle shipped in the Docker images of APM Server; Auditbeat, Filebeat, Heartbeat, Metricbeat and Packetbeat; Elastic Agent, including Fleet Server and Cloudbeat; Logstash, for TLS connections that use the operating system certificate bundle; Elastic connectors; Universal Profiling (host agent, collector and symbolizer); and Elastic Maps Server. This certificate bundle, a dependency of these products (Dependency on Vulnerable Third-Party Component, CWE-1395), could allow an attacker to intercept or modify TLS-protected traffic via Signature Spoofing by Key Theft (CAPEC-474). The certificate bundle includes root certificate authorities that signed eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities whose private keys are compromised. Anyone with these keys can issue a certificate for any host name that these products accept as trusted. Exploitation requires an attacker in a network position between the product and the remote party, who presents a certificate issued with one of the compromised keys.

cna.title: Forged signed tokens let any registered user take over other users and organizations

descriptions.value: A registered user can obtain a validly signed token with claims of their choosing and use it as a login session for another user, without knowing any identifier of the victim when database filter objects are used as claims.

An attacker can join any other organization as super administrator, using an organization id that is exposed by any shared post preview link, read its API key and channel list and schedule posts through its connected social accounts.
An attacker can reset the password of a user whose id they know, and can obtain an organization with a lifetime top-tier subscription through the enterprise provisioning endpoint.
Forged tokens do not expire and cannot be told apart from genuine ones.
The narrower invitation route lets a user who may invite team members repeatedly stop the scheduled posts of a channel of another organization, and lift the channel limit of their own plan.

exploits.value: Exploitation was demonstrated end to end against an unmodified backend build at commit 3a7d28b7ad96: a second self-registered user became super administrator of another user's organization and read its API key. Session, password reset, enterprise and subscription tokens obtained the same way were each accepted by their endpoints.

timeline.value: Anthropic has disclosed a thorough report of this vulnerability including a working PoC to Postiz
Postiz has reproduced the vulnerability and is working on a fix
Postiz has pushed a fix for this vulnerability and verified it
Postiz has created a release and published the advisory

workarounds.value: If you do not use channels that rely on the Postiz browser extension, block POST /integrations/extension-refresh at your reverse proxy. This removes the main signing route; the team invitation route remains.
Set DISABLE_REGISTRATION=true. The attacker needs an ordinary account, so closing self-registration limits exposure to people who already hold one. This reduces reach, it does not close the issue.

descriptions.value:
Postiz signs its session, invitation and password reset tokens with one shared secret and without any marker of what a token is for. A route that refreshes the credentials of a browser-extension channel signed data taken from the request itself and stored the result where the requesting user can read it back. A user could therefore obtain a validly signed token containing any claims they choose, which the application accepts as a session, as an organization invitation with a chosen role, as a password reset or as an enterprise provisioning token.

A second, narrower route that creates team invitations signs extra fields from the request body in the same way.

configurations.value: The instance must be able to reach api2.skool.com, as any instance using the Skool provider can. No setting has to be changed.

With Stripe billing configured, the attacker's own plan must allow one channel and the target organization must not be on the STANDARD tier. The session and password reset tokens are not affected by these limits.
Self-registration is open unless DISABLE_REGISTRATION is set to true.

cna.title: ONNX: Out-of-bounds read in ConvTranspose shape inference via undersized weight rank

descriptions.value: Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) is an open standard for machine learning interoperability. From 1.2.1 until 1.22.0, ConvTranspose shape inference processes a weight tensor with fewer than three dimensions without a kernel_shape attribute by deriving an empty effective_kernel_shape and indexing it for the input's spatial dimensions. The flaw affects convTransposeShapeInference_opset11() and the current inference path, and an untrusted model that can pass onnx.checker.check_model() can crash onnx.shape_inference.infer_shapes(), causing denial of service without demonstrated confidentiality or integrity impact. This issue is fixed in version 1.22.0.

descriptions.value: The VOD Infomaniak plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to authorization bypass in all versions up to, and including, 1.5.15. This is due to the plugin not properly verifying that a user is authorized to perform an action. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with subscriber-level access and above, to initiate unauthorized video imports using the site owner's Infomaniak API credentials, consume the site owner's VOD account quota, and insert arbitrary rows into the wp_vod_upload table causing public shortcodes to resolve to attacker-chosen video content. This action is explicitly reserved for Contributor-level and above by the plugin's own role-rights system, meaning subscriber access is intentionally forbidden by design — the AJAX handler simply omits the enforcement.

amount, regardless of how much was actually paid.

Missing token audience validation in the OAuth authentication mode of AWS API MCP Server before version 1.6.0 might allow local users to run AWS operations with the server's configured AWS credentials via an access token issued to another application by the same identity provider.



To remediate this issue, users should upgrade to version 1.6.0 and configure the expected token audience or client ID for the server.

cna.title: NULL pointer dereference in the BSD raw IPv6 send path when the destination table is full

descriptions.value: In Eclipse ThreadX NetX Duo versions 6.0 through 6.5.2.202603a, built with BSD raw socket and IPv6 support, the IPv6 raw send path uses the destination-table entry it adds without checking that the add succeeded. When the destination table is full and an off-link destination is reached through a default router whose neighbour cache entry is unknown, sending on an IPv6 raw socket with header inclusion dereferences a NULL pointer; a remote sender can fill the table, for example with ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages, and crash the sending thread.

cna.title: vLLM: Out-of-vocabulary prompt token id passes input validation and triggers a CUDA device-side assert (engine crash / DoS)

descriptions.value: vLLM is an inference and serving engine for large language models. Prior to 0.32.0, vllm/tokenizers/hf.py computes max_token_id with an off-by-one upper bound, allowing a pre-tokenized prompt ID equal to the vocabulary size to pass validation. For a tensor-parallel size of one and an exact multiple-of-64 vocabulary, VocabParallelEmbedding.forward does not mask that value before F.embedding uses it, causing a CUDA device-side assertion and terminating the engine. This issue is fixed in version 0.32.0.

references.name: `Ash.bulk_create` with `return_skipped_upsert?: true` in AshPostgres returns another tenant's record for a skipped upsert

descriptions.value:
Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in ash-project ash_postgres allows a user to read another tenant's record through a skipped upsert.

When Ash.bulk_create/4 or a single create runs as an upsert with return_skipped_upsert?: true and the upsert is skipped (for example because its upsert_condition does not hold), AshPostgres.DataLayer reads the existing row back by the upsert identity in do_bulk_create/3 and upsert/4. That lookup did not apply the resource's attribute multitenancy, so on a resource using strategy :attribute it could match and return the row of another tenant with the same identity values, exposing its fields to the caller.

This issue affects ash_postgres: from 2.6.22 before 2.15.2.

cna.title: Stanza: RCE via pickle deserialization in the lemmatizer

descriptions.value: Stanza is a Stanford NLP Python library for tokenization, sentence segmentation, NER, and parsing of many human languages. From 1.14.0 until 1.15.0, loading an attacker-supplied lemmatizer checkpoint can execute arbitrary code because stanza/models/lemma/trainer.py stores pos_dict as gzip-compressed pickle bytes and Trainer.load passes the decompressed stream to unrestricted pickle.loads. The outer torch.load call uses weights_only=True, but the nested bytes are treated as a primitive and are not inspected by that allowlist. The path is reachable during pipeline construction through a caller-influenced lemma_model_path, before inference begins. This issue is fixed in version 1.15.0.

descriptions.value: OpenBao before 2.6.4 and 2.7.x before 2.7.1 contains a flaw in its rate limit quota subsystem where role resolution fails for requests with form-encoded bodies or forwarded certificates, so quota rules scoped to backend-specific roles are not enforced. Valid callers can repeatedly issue tokens without consuming the configured role-based rate limit budget.

cna.title: Spreadsheet::XLSX versions before 0.19 for Perl allow code execution via string eval of number format conditions in ExcelFmt

solutions.value: Upgrade to Spreadsheet-XLSX 0.19 or later.

descriptions.value:
Spreadsheet::XLSX versions before 0.19 for Perl allow code execution via string eval of number format conditions in ExcelFmt.

When a number format has a condition such as [>100], ExcelFmt chooses the format section by passing the condition and the cell value to a string eval. Both come from the workbook, and the eval runs while Spreadsheet::XLSX->new parses it.

An attacker who supplies an XLSX file can run arbitrary Perl code.
